# SIRUP - full documentation

<!-- source: docs/index.md -->

# SIRUP: Spatial Immune Receptor Utilities Package

<div markdown="1" style="background: #9e584a; padding: 12px; margin-bottom: 24px; line-height: 24px;">
  <p style="margin: -12px -12px 12px; padding: 6px 12px; background: #8b3620; color: #ffffff; font-weight: 700;">Under construction</p>
  This site is still under construction. Be aware that some information may be missing or incorrect.
</div>

<img src="img/sirup-logo.png" alt="SIRUP logo" align="right" width="130" style="margin: 0 0 12px 24px;">
SIRUP, the Spatial Immune Receptor Utilities Package, is an R package for working with
spatial adaptive immune receptor repertoire sequencing (spAIRR-seq) data. 
It works with B cell receptor (BCR) and T cell receptor
(TCR) sequences that have a spatial barcode, together with spatial gene
expression from the same tissue section. Isn't that sweet?

SIRUP helps you:

1. **Process.** Convert demultiplexed long-read spatial immune receptor sequences 
   into high-quality consensus receptor sequences for each spatial location.
   Outputs an [AIRR rearrangement style table](https://docs.airr-community.org/en/latest/datarep/rearrangements.html).
2. **Integrate.** Combine spatially-resolved immune receptors and a Seurat spatial
   transcriptomics object into one unified SIRUP object. The SIRUP object can hold
   multiple spatial tissue sections, as well as associated non-spatial AIRR-seq data
   from bulk or single-cell experiments.
3. **Analyze and visualize.** Select regions of interest through *in silico* micro-dissection,
   measure clonal dominance and diversity within ROIs, test spatial patterns,
   build lineage trees and visualize them over tissue, and more!

<div markdown="1" style="background: #ffedcc; padding: 12px; margin-bottom: 24px; line-height: 24px;">
  <p style="margin: -12px -12px 12px; padding: 6px 12px; background: #d6b676; color: #ffffff; font-weight: 700;">Did you know?</p>
  Maple syrup has been spelled [maple sirup](https://maplesyruphistory.com/2022/09/04/the-origins-of-the-spelling-of-maple-sirup-with-an-i/) at different points of U.S. history.
</div>

## Getting started

Start with [Get started with SIRUP](vignettes/get-started.md). It takes about 15
minutes and uses example data that comes with the package. You build a SIRUP
object, plot receptors on the tissue, and measure clonal dominance in a region.

Install SIRUP from GitHub with BiocManager, which will also install dependencies:

```r
if (!requireNamespace("BiocManager", quietly = TRUE)) install.packages("BiocManager")
BiocManager::install("hoehnlab/SIRUP")
```

Use R 4.1 or later.

## For AI agents and LLMs

SIRUP provides the following resources for AI agents. See the [guide](vignettes/llm-agents.md) for more details.

* [llms.txt](https://github.com/hoehnlab/SIRUP/blob/main/llms.txt) is a short Markdown index of the SIRUP documentation, with links.
* [llms-full.txt](https://github.com/hoehnlab/SIRUP/blob/main/llms-full.txt) holds the whole documentation in one text file.
* [llms.json](https://github.com/hoehnlab/SIRUP/blob/main/llms.json) is the same index as JSON. It lists each tutorial, guide, and function, with a summary and links.
* [llms-full.json](https://github.com/hoehnlab/SIRUP/blob/main/llms-full.json) holds the whole documentation as JSON, with the full text of each page.
* The **SIRUP skill** teaches an agent how to use SIRUP: how to build an object, which function answers which question, and which checks to run. Find the skill in `inst/skills/sirup`, and install it as shown below.

**Set up the skill**

Install SIRUP. Then use the `installSIRUPSkill()` function to install the skill for your agent. Currently,  `installSIRUPSkill` is set up to work for Claude Code, Codex, or Antigravity. Other types of agents can be set up by manually installing the skill.

```r
library(SIRUP)
installSIRUPSkill("claude")   # or "codex" or "antigravity"
```

By default, this installs the skill for the agent for all projects. To install the skill for one project only, give 
the skills folder of the project, for example `installSIRUPSkill("claude", install_dir = ".claude/skills")`.
Then start a new session and ensure that the SIRUP skill is available.

<!-- source: docs/vignettes/choose-spatial-statistic.md -->

Choose the right spatial statistic for your question
================

This guide helps you choose an appropriate spatial statistic to answer
the question you want to ask. Each section below names one question. It
then gives the function, the input, and how to understand the results.

A few definitions: A *spot* is spatially-resolved location where we
capture gene expression or a BCR/TCR sequence. A *clone* is a group of
cells that are inferred to descend from a common ancestor. *Spatial
autocorrelation* is the tendency of nearby spots to have similar values,
i.e., high values by high values and low values by low values.

All tests need a SIRUP object, or a Seurat object with spatial images.
The tests read the spot coordinates from the object. Most tests compare
each spot with its “neighbors”. Generally, you can set the number of
neighbors with `k` (i.e., the `k` nearest spots will be neighbors) or
`radius` (which draws a circle with radius `radius` around the point in
question and all points inside that circle are neighbors of the point).

## Match the question to the function

| Question | Function | Input |
|----|----|----|
| Is a continuous variable spatially autocorrelated? | `spatialMoran()` | One gene or numeric metadata column |
| Where is a continuous variable spatially autocorrelated? | `spatialLocalMoran()` | One gene or numeric metadata column |
| Do two continuous variables co-vary in space? | `spatialLee()` | Two continuous variables |
| How far does a clone spread? | `spatialCloneSpread()` | Receptor table with clone IDs, pass the ID of the clone you’re interested in |
| Is a discrete variable (in this case a particular clone) spatially autocorrelated? | `spatialCloneJoinCount()` | Receptor table with clone IDs, pass the ID of the clone you’re interested in |
| Do two discrete variables co-vary in space? | `spatialRipleyCrossK()` | One metadata column with two labels |

## Load the example object

The examples use one myasthenia gravis (MG) thymus section. This code
downloads a saved SIRUP object for it, which is not part of the SIRUP
package, and reads it. The object has BCRs and TCRs, cell-type
estimates, and BCR clones. Change `dest` to a folder you want to keep.
The function skips files that are already there. To see how the object
was built, see [Get started with SIRUP](get-started.md).

``` r
extdata <- SIRUP::downloadSIRUPExample(
  dest = file.path(tempdir(), "SIRUP_example"),
  files = "mg_thymus_slice2_brighter.sirup.rds"
)
#> ℹ Downloading 'mg_thymus_slice2_brighter.sirup.rds'
```

``` r
library(SIRUP)
library(dplyr)

x <- readSIRUP(file.path(extdata, "mg_thymus_slice2_brighter.sirup.rds"))
x
#> <SIRUP object>
#> Spatial data:    Seurat, 3,203 spatial IDs, 449 genes, 1 image
#> Receptor data:   2 slots
#>   BCR: 2,105 receptor sequences x 57 columns; 797/868 receptor IDs in spatial data (91.8%)
#>   TCR: 3,610 receptor sequences x 56 columns; 1,414/1,571 receptor IDs in spatial data (90.0%)
#> Spatial ID field: barcode_10x
#> Clone ID field:  clone_id
#> Analyses:        0
```

## Is a continuous variable spatially autocorrelated?

Use `spatialMoran()` to determine if a continuous variable is spatially
autocorrelated, i.e., if neighboring spots have similar values. This
function computes [Moran’s
I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moran%27s_I#Global_Moran's_I). Moran’s
I is near 0 when the values show no spatial pattern, it is positive when
similar values are nearby, and it is negative when dissimilar values are
nearby.

The input is a SIRUP or Seurat object. `variable_type` tells the
function what type of variable it is: a gene (`"feature"`) or a numeric
metadata column (`"metadata"`). `k` is the number of neighbors.

The estimate $I$ and the associated p value are reported. Note that a
larger section can inflate significance, so you may see a tiny p value
for a weak pattern in larger datasets.

See the code below for an example on the thymus section.

``` r
moran <- spatialMoran(
  x,
  variable = "GC B",
  variable_type = "metadata",
  k = 6
)
#> Loading required namespace: Seurat
moran$test$estimate[[1]]
#> [1] 0.6229165
moran$test$p.value
#> [1] 0
```

## **Where** is a continuous variable spatially autocorrelated?

Use `spatialLocalMoran()` to find where a continuous variable is
spatially autocorrelated, i.e., which spots sit in a cluster of similar
values. This function computes [local Moran’s
I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moran%27s_I#Local_Moran's_I) (also
called LISA) for each spot. Local Moran’s I is positive when a spot has
neighbors with similar values and negative when a spot differs from its
neighbors.

The input is a SIRUP or Seurat object. `variable_type` tells the
function what type of variable it is: a gene (`"feature"`) or a numeric
metadata column (`"metadata"`). `k` is the number of neighbors.

The result has one row for each spot, with the local I (`local_i`), a
z-score (`z_i`), and a p value (`p_value`). Each spot has its own p
value, so we should adjust for multiple testing.
`plotSpatialLocalMoran()` draws the z-scores on the tissue.

See the code below for an example on the thymus section.

``` r
local_moran <- spatialLocalMoran(
  x,
  variable = "GC B",
  variable_type = "metadata",
  k = 6
)
head(local_moran[, c("cell", "local_i", "z_i", "p_value")])
#>                 cell    local_i       z_i     p_value
#> 1 AAACAAGTATCTCCCA-1 0.42119564 1.8775350 0.060444809
#> 2 AAACACCAATAACTGC-1 0.02554433 0.1780355 0.858695126
#> 3 AAACAGCTTTCAGAAG-1 0.67548360 2.1434191 0.032079462
#> 4 AAACAGGGTCTATATT-1 0.44557822 1.5436247 0.122679267
#> 5 AAACAGTGTTCCTGGG-1 0.10316582 0.6444111 0.519308914
#> 6 AAACATGGTGAGAGGA-1 2.05891309 3.0435870 0.002337758
plotSpatialLocalMoran(x, local_moran, point_size = 1)
```

![](choose-spatial-statistic_files/figure-gfm/local-moran-1.jpeg)

## Do two continuous variables co-vary in space?

Use `spatialLee()` to determine if two continuous variables share a
spatial pattern, i.e., if a high value of one variable tends to sit near
high values of the other. This function computes [Lee’s
L](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lee%27s_L). Lee’s L is near 0 when the
variables show no shared pattern, it is positive when both variables are
high (or both low) in the same neighborhoods, and it is negative when
one variable is high where the other is low.

The input is a SIRUP object or a Seurat object. `x` and `y` are the
names of the two variables, and `x_type` and `y_type` tell the function
what type each variable is: a gene (`"feature"`) or a numeric metadata
column (`"metadata"`). `k` is the number of neighbors.

The estimate $L$ and the associated p value are reported. The default
test (`method = "analytical"`) builds a dense matrix with one entry for
each pair of spots, so it needs a lot of memory for large datasets. For
large data, such as Visium HD, set `method = "mc"` to use a permutation
test.

See the code below for an example on the thymus section.

``` r
lee <- spatialLee(
  x,
  x = "AICDA", x_type = "feature",
  y = "MS4A1", y_type = "feature",
  assay = "Spatial", layer = "data",
  k = 6
)
lee$L
#> [1] 0.09748529
lee$test$p.value
#> [1] 2.174023e-49
```

## How far does a clone spread?

Use `spatialCloneSpread()` to determine how far clones spread across the
tissue, i.e., how far apart their or sequences are. This function is
just descriptive. For each clone, it computes the distance between every
pair of points and reports the mean and the maximum of those distances.

The input is a SIRUP object or receptor table with clone IDs and spatial
IDs. A clone needs at least `min_spatial_ids` points (default 2). By
default, each sequence is a point, so sequences in the same spot give
distances of 0. Set `collapse_within_spot = TRUE` to count each spot
once.

The result has one row for each sample and clone, with the number of
spots (`n_spatial_ids`), the mean distance (`mean_pairwise_distance`),
and the maximum distance (`max_pairwise_distance`). Distances are in
image pixels.

See the code below for an example on the thymus section.

``` r
spread <- spatialCloneSpread(x, slot = "BCR", min_spatial_ids = 3)
spread %>%
  arrange(desc(n_spatial_ids)) %>%
  head()
#> # A tibble: 6 × 5
#>   sample  clone_id n_spatial_ids mean_pairwise_distance max_pairwise_distance
#>   <chr>   <chr>            <int>                  <dbl>                 <dbl>
#> 1 spatial 34                  86                   66.2                 397. 
#> 2 spatial 288                 42                  123.                  304. 
#> 3 spatial 196                 38                  156.                  395. 
#> 4 spatial 739                 16                   21.5                  75.1
#> 5 spatial 810                 14                   80.0                 263. 
#> 6 spatial 907                 14                   54.2                 120.
```

## Is a discrete variable (i.e., a particular clone) spatially autocorrelated?

Use `spatialCloneJoinCount()` to determine if a discrete variable is
spatially autocorrelated. This function computes the [join count
statistic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Join_count_statistic). Here,
the variable is whether a spot holds a particular clone, i.e., if the
spots of a clone sit next to each other. This function marks the spots
that hold the clone, counts the neighbor pairs in which both spots hold
the clone (the joins), and compares that count with the count expected
by chance. The observed count is higher than expected when the sequences
in the clone stay nearby each other.

The input is a SIRUP object receptor table with clone IDs and spatial
IDs. By default, the function tests every clone that occurs in at least
`min_spatial_ids` spots. Give `clone_val` to test chosen clones. If the
object has stored polygons, the function runs one test for each polygon.
Set `use_stored_polygons = FALSE` to run one test over the entire
section in this case.

The `summary` table has one row for each clone, with the observed and
expected join counts, a z-score (`statistic`), and a p value
(`p_value`). The default alternative is `"greater"`, so the test looks
for more joins than chance. The function tests many clones at once, so
be sure to adjust for multiple testing.

See the code below for an example on the thymus section.

``` r
big_clones <- getReceptors(x, slot = "BCR") %>%
  filter(!is.na(barcode_10x)) %>%
  distinct(clone_id, barcode_10x) %>%
  count(clone_id, sort = TRUE) %>%
  slice_head(n = 5) %>%
  pull(clone_id)

join_count <- spatialCloneJoinCount(
  x,
  slot = "BCR",
  clone_val = big_clones,
  use_stored_polygons = FALSE,
  k = 6,
  return_data = TRUE
)
join_count$summary[, c("clone_id", "observed_join_count", "expected_join_count", "p_value")]
#>   clone_id observed_join_count expected_join_count      p_value
#> 1      598                12.5           0.4145729 1.855757e-89
#> 2      288                30.0           2.6457286 1.118248e-74
#> 3       34                67.5          16.1683417 1.117067e-47
#> 4       64                 5.5           0.3391960 1.842208e-21
#> 5      196                15.5           2.6457286 4.997114e-18

plotSpatialCloneJoinCount(
  join_count = join_count,
  object = x,
  clone_val = join_count$summary$clone_id[[1]],
  show_neighbors = TRUE
)
```

![](choose-spatial-statistic_files/figure-gfm/join-count-1.jpeg)

## Do two discrete variables co-vary in space?

Use `spatialRipleyCrossK()` to determine if two discrete variables
co-vary in space, i.e., if spots of type A lie near spots of type B.
This function computes [Ripley’s cross
K](https://academicweb.nd.edu/~mhaenggi/ee87021/Dixon-K-Function.pdf?utm_campaign=redirect&utm_medium=web&utm_source=www3.nd.edu).
It counts the spots of type B within each distance of an average spot of
type A. It then compares that curve with curves from random relabeling
of the spots, which gives an envelope. Ripley’s cross K is similar to
Lee’s L, but it works with discrete data rather than continuous.

The input is a SIRUP object or a Seurat object with a column that holds
the labels (`mark_col`). Give the two levels to compare as `i` and `j`.
Set `nsim` above 0 to generate the randomly relabeled envelope for
comparison. Spots with `NA` in the column are left out.

The result holds the observed K at each distance (`plot_data`). A curve
above the envelope (which represents the null distribution created by
permuting labels) means that A and B are nearer than expected by chance,
i.e., they **colocalize**. A curve below the envelope means that A and B
are farther apart than expected by chance. `plotRipleyCrossK()` plots
the curve and the envelope. The distance is in image pixels at the
stored `image_scale`.

See the code below for an example on the thymus section.

``` r
# Label spots with mostly GC B cells or mostly T follicular helper (Tfh) cells.
x <- updateSpatial(x, function(spatial) {
  gc_b <- spatial$`GC B` > 0.10
  tfh <- spatial$Tfh > 0.10
  spatial$gc_tfh_mark <- case_when(
    gc_b & !tfh ~ "GC B",
    tfh & !gc_b ~ "Tfh",
    TRUE ~ NA_character_
  )
  spatial
})

set.seed(1)
kcross <- spatialRipleyCrossK(
  x,
  mark_col = "gc_tfh_mark",
  i = "GC B",
  j = "Tfh",
  nsim = 39,
  max_r = 40
)
plotRipleyCrossK(kcross, title = "Cross K: GC B spots to Tfh spots")
```

![](choose-spatial-statistic_files/figure-gfm/ripley-1.jpeg)

<!-- source: docs/vignettes/clones-and-trees.md -->

Infer clones and lineage trees in situ
================

<div markdown="1"
style="background: #F7E5BC; padding: 12px; margin-bottom: 24px; line-height: 24px;">

<p style="margin: -12px -12px 12px; padding: 6px 12px; background: #d6b676; color: #ffffff; font-weight: 700;">

<b>Note</b>
</p>

**Time:** ~15 minutes.<br> **Data:** The example SIRUP object, plus its
polygon file.<br>

</div>

Here, we will work with the clones in a SIRUP object, build lineage
trees for some of them, and pair each tree with the tissue.

A *clone* is a group of B or T cells that descend from one ancestor cell
and share its receptor rearrangement. A *lineage tree* shows how the
sequences of one clone relate to each other, where each tip is one
sequence. Pairing a tree with the tissue shows where each tip sits. At
the end, we will compare distances in the tree with distances on the
tissue.

SIRUP does not reimplement clone calling or tree building. It runs the
Immcantation tools (scoper, dowser, shazam) on the receptor table inside
the SIRUP object, then adds the spatial part: clone maps, trees paired
with tissue plots, and distances between tips in and between regions.

<div markdown="1"
style="background: #F7E5BC; padding: 12px; margin-bottom: 24px; line-height: 24px;">

<p style="margin: -12px -12px 12px; padding: 6px 12px; background: #d6b676; color: #ffffff; font-weight: 700;">

<b>Note</b>
</p>

This page starts with a saved SIRUP object, which is loaded below. To
learn how the object is built, see
[Get started with SIRUP](get-started.md). To learn about the
polygons used here, see [Annotate tissue ROIs and analyze local clonal structure](regions.md).

</div>

## Get the example data

This page uses example files that are slightly too big to be part of the
SIRUP package. This code downloads them. Change `dest` to a folder you
want to keep. The function skips files that are already there.

``` r
extdata <- SIRUP::downloadSIRUPExample(
  dest = file.path(tempdir(), "SIRUP_example"),
  files = c(
    "mg_thymus_slice2_brighter.sirup.rds",
    "mg_thymus_slice2_gc_polygons.csv"
  )
)
#> ℹ 'mg_thymus_slice2_brighter.sirup.rds' is already in '/scratch/f007p0j/RtmpscrZTE/SIRUP_example'.
#> ℹ Downloading 'mg_thymus_slice2_gc_polygons.csv'
```

``` r
library(SIRUP)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
```

``` r
sirup <- readSIRUP(file.path(extdata, "mg_thymus_slice2_brighter.sirup.rds"))
sirup
#> <SIRUP object>
#> Spatial data:    Seurat, 3,203 spatial IDs, 449 genes, 1 image
#> Receptor data:   2 slots
#>   BCR: 2,105 receptor sequences x 57 columns; 797/868 receptor IDs in spatial data (91.8%)
#>   TCR: 3,610 receptor sequences x 56 columns; 1,414/1,571 receptor IDs in spatial data (90.0%)
#> Spatial ID field: barcode_10x
#> Clone ID field:  clone_id
#> Analyses:        0
```

The object holds two receptor slots, `"BCR"` and `"TCR"`, and the
functions that interact with the receptors in the SIRUP object read one
slot at a time. If we only need to work with one type of receptor, we
can specify the slot in the function call.

In [Annotate tissue ROIs and analyze local clonal structure](regions.md), we annotated regions of
interest (ROIs) in the tissue. We can add the polygons that outline
these ROIs to the SIRUP object so that we can include them in plots and
analyses. Add the polygons to the object with `addPolygons()`.

``` r
sirup <- addPolygons(
  sirup,
  polygons_path = file.path(extdata, "mg_thymus_slice2_gc_polygons.csv")
)
```

## Build clones

A clone, or clonal lineage, is a set of cells inferred to have descended
from a common ancestor. We can infer clones from the receptor sequences
using `scoper::hierarchicalClones()` for B cells and
`scoper::identicalClones()` for T cells. Use the `updateReceptors()`
function to run a function on the receptor table in a SIRUP object and
update the object with the result.

The example object already has BCR clones from
[Get started with SIRUP](get-started.md). To start from scratch, we
will remove the `clone_id` column and clear the clone field first.

``` r
sirup <- updateReceptors(
  sirup,
  dplyr::select,
  -clone_id,
  slot = "BCR", # specify the receptor slot
  receptor_fields = list(clone = NULL)
)
```

Then build the clones.

``` r
sirup <- updateReceptors(
  sirup,
  scoper::hierarchicalClones,
  slot = "BCR",
  threshold = 0.1,
  summarize_clones = FALSE,
  nproc = 1
)
#> Warning: package 'scoper' was built under R version 4.5.3

sirup
#> <SIRUP object>
#> Spatial data:    Seurat, 3,203 spatial IDs, 449 genes, 1 image
#> Receptor data:   2 slots
#>   BCR: 2,105 receptor sequences x 67 columns; 797/868 receptor IDs in spatial data (91.8%)
#>   TCR: 3,610 receptor sequences x 66 columns; 1,414/1,571 receptor IDs in spatial data (90.0%)
#> Spatial ID field: barcode_10x
#> Clone ID field:  clone_id
#> Analyses:        0
#> Polygons:        9
```

Because T cells do not mutate their TCRs, clones are called with
`scoper::identicalClones()`, as is below.

``` r
sirup <- updateReceptors(
  sirup,
  scoper::identicalClones,
  slot = "TCR",
  summarize_clones = FALSE,
  nproc = 1
)
```

## Reconstruct clonal germlines

Next, reconstruct the germline of the B cell clones with
`dowser::createGermlines()`. The germline is the sequence of the
unmutated common ancestor, which will root the reconstructed trees.
Building the germline requires IMGT references. Set the variable
`imgt_dir` to the folder that contains them.

<div markdown="1"
style="background: #F7E5BC; padding: 12px; margin-bottom: 24px; line-height: 24px;">

<p style="margin: -12px -12px 12px; padding: 6px 12px; background: #d6b676; color: #ffffff; font-weight: 700;">

<b>Note</b>
</p>

If you have not yet set up the IMGT references, see the
[documentation](https://github.com/hoehnlab/airrblast) for the
`airrblast` package and download and set up the IMGT references.

</div>

``` r
references <- dowser::readIMGT(imgt_dir)
#> [1] "Read in 1198 from 17 fasta files"

sirup <- updateReceptors(
  sirup,
  dowser::createGermlines,
  slot = "BCR",
  references = references,
  id = "sequence_id",
  nproc = 1
)
```

To be safe, we can also filter out potential PCR chimeras using
`shazam::slideWindowDb()`.

``` r
sirup <- updateReceptors(sirup, slot = "BCR", function(receptors) {
  chimera <- shazam::slideWindowDb(
    receptors,
    sequenceColumn = "sequence_alignment",
    germlineColumn = "germline_alignment_d_mask",
    mutThresh = 6,
    windowSize = 10
  )
  receptors[!chimera, ]
})
```

## Estimate somatic hypermutation levels

Use `shazam::observedMutations()` to count the SHM levels of each
sequence against the germline.

``` r
sirup <- updateReceptors(
  sirup,
  shazam::observedMutations,
  slot = "BCR",
  sequenceColumn = "sequence_alignment",
  germlineColumn = "germline_alignment_d_mask",
  frequency = TRUE,
  combine = TRUE
)
summary(getReceptors(sirup, slot = "BCR")$mu_freq) # SHM frequency stored in mu_freq column
#>    Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max. 
#> 0.00000 0.01493 0.03727 0.04165 0.06377 0.13814
```

`plotReceptors()` can color spots by a numeric column in the receptor
data. Pass the column to `value`. If a spot has several receptors,
`value_combine` sets how SIRUP combines them (default is `"mean"`).

``` r
plotReceptors(
  sirup,
  slot = "BCR",
  group = "locus",
  value = "mu_freq",
  value_colors = c("white", "darkred"),
  value_combine = "mean",
  receptor_size = 1.3,
  polygons = TRUE,
  polygon_alpha = 0,
  polygon_color = "black",
  title = "Mean SHM frequency per spot"
)
```

![](clones-and-trees_files/figure-gfm/shm-map-1.jpeg)

## Infer trees

First, we need to choose a few clones to build trees for. The three
clones below are large and have sequences in the ectopic germinal
centers (the ROIs).

``` r
tree_clones <- c("739", "810", "196")

# Plot the locations of the three chosen clones
plotReceptors(
  sirup,
  slot = "BCR",
  group = "clone_id",
  group_val = tree_clones,
  receptor_size = 1.6,
  polygons = TRUE,
  polygon_alpha = 0.3,
  title = "Selected clones"
)
```

![](clones-and-trees_files/figure-gfm/choose-clones-1.jpeg)

To build trees with Dowser, we need a formatted clones object.
`formatSpatialClones()` wraps `dowser::formatClones()` but allows users
to provide a SIRUP object, and it automatically places a
`formatted_clones` object in the SIRUP object’s analysis slot. Then, we
can call `getSpatialTrees()`, which wraps `dowser::getTrees()` but
allows users to provide a SIRUP object, and puts the trees in the SIRUP
object’s analysis slot.

``` r
# Filter the SIRUP object to only include the tree clones
tree_sirup <- updateReceptors(sirup, dplyr::filter, clone_id %in% tree_clones, slot = "BCR")

tree_sirup <- formatSpatialClones(
  tree_sirup,
  slot = "BCR",
  analysis_name = "formatted_clones",
  id = "sequence_id",
  germ = "germline_alignment_d_mask",
  traits = c("barcode_10x", "polygon_id") # Make sure to set the barcode column as a trait so that you don't collapse
  # sequences with the same sequence that were observed in different locations.
)

set.seed(1)
tree_sirup <- getSpatialTrees(
  tree_sirup,
  slot = "BCR",
  f_clones_analysis = "formatted_clones",
  analysis_name = "trees",
  build = "pratchet"
)

trees <- getAnalysis(tree_sirup, "trees")
trees
#> # A tibble: 3 × 5
#>   clone_id data       locus  seqs trees  
#>   <chr>    <list>     <chr> <int> <list> 
#> 1 196      <airrClon> IGH      38 <phylo>
#> 2 739      <airrClon> IGH      15 <phylo>
#> 3 810      <airrClon> IGH      13 <phylo>
```

For more information on building trees, see the [Dowser
documentation](https://dowser.readthedocs.io/en/stable/vignettes/Building-Trees-Vignette/).

``` r
sirup <- setAnalysis(sirup, "trees", trees)
```

## Pair each tree with the tissue

`plotSpatialCloneTreePairs()` plots trees on the left and H&E images and
the locations of the tip sequences on the right. `color_by` allows you
to color the tips on the tree by a column in the receptor data, but
leaving it `NULL` gives each tip its own color.

``` r
pairs <- plotSpatialCloneTreePairs(
  getAnalysis(tree_sirup, "trees"),
  object = sirup,
  slot = "BCR",
  clone_val = tree_clones,
  id = "sequence_id",
  polygons = TRUE,
  polygon_alpha = 0,
  polygon_color = "black"
)
#> Warning: Using `size` aesthetic for lines was deprecated in ggplot2 3.4.0.
#> ℹ Please use `linewidth` instead.
#> ℹ The deprecated feature was likely used in the ggtree package.
#>   Please report the issue at <https://github.com/YuLab-SMU/ggtree/issues>.
#> This warning is displayed once per session.
#> Call `lifecycle::last_lifecycle_warnings()` to see where this warning was
#> generated.
names(pairs)
#> [1] "196" "739" "810"

pairs[[1]]
```

![](clones-and-trees_files/figure-gfm/tree-pairs-1.jpeg)

The result is a list with one element for each clone, and each element
consists of the tree on the left and the map on the right. Each element
also holds the `tree` plot and the `spatial_clone` plot, which can be
accessed separately for a custom layout. Sequences in the same spot
share a point on the map.

### Color tips by group

A clone with many tips can be hard to read when each tip has its own
color. `clusterTreesTips()` cuts each tree into `k` connected groups of
related tips. The code below uses `k = 4` for every tree. Then
`plotSpatialCloneTreePairs()` with `color_by = "tree_cluster"` colors
the tips by their corresponding cluster for easier visualization.

``` r
clustered <- clusterTreesTips(
  trees,
  k = 4,
  id = "sequence_id",
  cluster = "tree_cluster" # What column to store the cluster assignments in
)

cluster_pairs <- plotSpatialCloneTreePairs(
  clustered,
  object = sirup,
  slot = "BCR",
  clone_val = tree_clones,
  id = "sequence_id",
  color_by = "tree_cluster",
  polygons = TRUE,
  polygon_alpha = 0,
  polygon_color = "black",
  show_spatial_legend = FALSE
)

cluster_pairs[[1]]
```

![](clones-and-trees_files/figure-gfm/tree-clusters-1.jpeg)

`color_by` accepts any column of the dowser clone data. For example,
`color_by = "polygon_id"` colors each tip by which polygon it belongs
to.

<div markdown="1"
style="background: #F7E5BC; padding: 12px; margin-bottom: 24px; line-height: 24px;">

<p style="margin: -12px -12px 12px; padding: 6px 12px; background: #d6b676; color: #ffffff; font-weight: 700;">

<b>Tip</b>
</p>

`spatialCloneTreePairsToPDF(cluster_pairs, "tree_pairs.pdf")` plots one
page per clone and saves the results to a PDF file.

</div>

  [Process demultiplexed reads](processing.md).

  [Analyze multiple spatial sections and bulk BCR-seq](multisample.md).
- To test spatial patterns, read
  [Choose the right spatial statistic for your question](choose-spatial-statistic.md).

<!-- source: docs/vignettes/get-started.md -->

Get started with SIRUP
================

<div markdown="1"
style="background: #F7E5BC; padding: 12px; margin-bottom: 24px; line-height: 24px;">

<p style="margin: -12px -12px 12px; padding: 6px 12px; background: #d6b676; color: #ffffff; font-weight: 700;">

<b>Note</b>
</p>

**Time:** ~15 minutes.<br> **Data:** example spatial MG thymus data in
SIRUP.

</div>

Here, we will build a SIRUP object from example data and run a few
simple analyses.

<div markdown="1"
style="background: #F7E5BC; padding: 12px; margin-bottom: 24px; line-height: 24px;">

<p style="margin: -12px -12px 12px; padding: 6px 12px; background: #d6b676; color: #ffffff; font-weight: 700;">

<b>Note</b>
</p>

This page starts after read processing. If you have raw or demultiplexed
reads, see [Process demultiplexed reads](processing.md) first.

</div>

## Get the example data

This page uses example files that are slightly too big to be part of the
SIRUP package. This code downloads them. Change `dest` to a folder you
want to keep. The default folder is temporary. The function skips files
that are already there.

``` r
extdata <- SIRUP::downloadSIRUPExample(
  dest = file.path(tempdir(), "SIRUP_example"),
  files = c(
  "mg_thymus_slice2_spatial_brighter.rds",
  "mg_thymus_slice2_bcr.tsv.gz",
  "mg_thymus_slice2_tcr.tsv.gz",
  "mg_thymus_slice2_gc_polygons.csv",
  "mg_thymus_cell_types.csv.gz"
  )
)
#> ℹ Downloading 'mg_thymus_slice2_spatial_brighter.rds'
#> ℹ Downloading 'mg_thymus_slice2_bcr.tsv.gz'
#> ℹ Downloading 'mg_thymus_slice2_tcr.tsv.gz'
#> ℹ 'mg_thymus_slice2_gc_polygons.csv' is already in '/scratch/f007p0j/RtmpscrZTE/SIRUP_example'.
#> ℹ Downloading 'mg_thymus_cell_types.csv.gz'
```

## Install SIRUP

Install SIRUP and its dependencies from GitHub with BiocManager:

``` r
if (!requireNamespace("BiocManager", quietly = TRUE)) install.packages("BiocManager")
BiocManager::install("hoehnlab/SIRUP")
```

This vignette uses a few of SIRUP’s suggested packages as well. Run the
code below to install any that are missing:

``` r
packages <- c("spatstat.explore", "spatstat.geom", "spatstat.random", "pals")
missing <- packages[!vapply(packages, requireNamespace, logical(1), quietly = TRUE)]
if (length(missing) > 0) install.packages(missing)
```

## Look at the example data

SIRUP includes an example spAIRR-seq data set from the thymus of a
patient with myasthenia gravis (MG). The thymus in MG can contain
ectopic germinal centers (eGCs) where B cells undergo affinity
maturation. The data were generated with 10x Visium for spatial
transcriptomics and barcodes, then RAGE-seq + long-read Oxford Nanopore
sequencing to amplify BCRs/TCRs and sequence them.

This vignette uses these files:

| File | Contents |
|----|----|
| `mg_thymus_slice2_spatial_brighter.rds` | A spatial Seurat object for MG thymus |
| `mg_thymus_slice2_bcr.tsv.gz` | AIRR rearrangement table of IGH sequences with spatial IDs |
| `mg_thymus_slice2_tcr.tsv.gz` | AIRR rearrangement table of TRB sequences with spatial IDs |
| `mg_thymus_slice2_gc_polygons.csv` | Annotated polygons of the eGCs |
| `mg_thymus_cell_types.csv.gz` | Cell-type proportions for each spot |

The code above downloaded these files with `downloadSIRUPExample()`.

The SIRUP paper describes how the authors made these files. To reduce
file sizes, each Seurat object holds a few hundred genes and a reduced
image.

``` r
library(SIRUP)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
```

## Load the spatial GEX data and the receptors

Read the Seurat object and the AIRR table:

``` r
thymus <- readRDS(file.path(extdata, "mg_thymus_slice2_spatial_brighter.rds"))
thymus
#> An object of class Seurat 
#> 506 features across 3203 samples within 2 assays 
#> Active assay: Spatial (449 features, 0 variable features)
#>  2 layers present: counts, data
#>  1 other assay present: alra
#>  1 spatial field of view present: thymus_slice2

bcrs <- airr::read_rearrangement(file.path(extdata, "mg_thymus_slice2_bcr.tsv.gz"))
bcrs %>%
  select(sequence_id, v_call, j_call, c_call, sequence_alignment) %>%
  head()
#> # A tibble: 6 × 5
#>   sequence_id         v_call                    j_call c_call sequence_alignment
#>   <chr>               <chr>                     <chr>  <chr>  <chr>             
#> 1 9,TGATTCCCGGTTACCT  IGHV2-5*02                IGHJ4… IGHG1  ...ATCACCTTGAAGGA…
#> 2 11,TGATTCCCGGTTACCT IGHV3-30*03,IGHV3-30*06   IGHJ4… IGHG1  .................…
#> 3 2,TGATTCCCGGTTACCT  IGHV5-51*01               IGHJ5… IGHG2  GAGGTGCCGCTGGTGCA…
#> 4 6,TGATTCCCGGTTACCT  IGHV5-51*01               IGHJ5… IGHG2  GAGGTGCCGCTGGTGCA…
#> 5 5,CCTACATTCACAGACG  IGHV3-23*01,IGHV3-23*04,… IGHJ4… IGHG1  .................…
#> 6 3,CCTACATTCACAGACG  IGHV1-2*02,IGHV1-2*04     IGHJ4… IGHG1  CAGGTGCATCTGGTGCA…

tcrs <- airr::read_rearrangement(file.path(extdata, "mg_thymus_slice2_tcr.tsv.gz"))
```

Each row is one BCR or TCR sequence. The processing pipeline wrote the
spatial ID at the end of `sequence_id`, after a comma.

## Match each sequence to a spot

`extractSpatialIds()` is a convenience function to extract the spatial
ID and put it into its own column. The `regex` argument finds the
spatial ID. The `suffix` argument adds `-1`, so that each spatial ID
matches a spot name in the Seurat object.

``` r
bcrs <- extractSpatialIds(
  bcrs,
  id = "sequence_id",
  spatial_id = "barcode_10x",
  regex = ",([ACGT]{16})$",
  suffix = "-1"
)
tcrs <- extractSpatialIds(
  tcrs,
  id = "sequence_id",
  spatial_id = "barcode_10x",
  regex = ",([ACGT]{16})$",
  suffix = "-1"
)

head(colnames(thymus))
#> [1] "AAACAAGTATCTCCCA-1" "AAACACCAATAACTGC-1" "AAACAGCTTTCAGAAG-1"
#> [4] "AAACAGGGTCTATATT-1" "AAACAGTGTTCCTGGG-1" "AAACATGGTGAGAGGA-1"
mean(bcrs$barcode_10x %in% colnames(thymus))
#> [1] 0.9372528
mean(tcrs$barcode_10x %in% colnames(thymus))
#> [1] 0.9176248
```

A few sequences have a spatial ID that is not in the Seurat object. The
spot was likely off the tissue or failed the expression quality control.
SIRUP will maintain these receptor sequences in the integrated SIRUP
object, but it will not be able to place them in spatial plots.

## Filter the sequences

Keep only the high-quality sequences. The thresholds used are discussed
in [Process demultiplexed reads](processing.md).

``` r
bcrs <- filterAirr(
  bcrs,
  locus_val = "IGH",
  min_v_length = 250,
  min_j_length = 30,
  min_junction_length = 10,
  productive_only = TRUE,
  min_consensus_count = NULL,
  spatial_id = "barcode_10x"
)
#> filterAirr kept 2189 of 3793 rows (dropped 1604).

tcrs <- filterAirr(
  tcrs,
  locus_val = "TRB",
  min_v_length = 250,
  min_j_length = 30,
  min_junction_length = 10,
  productive_only = TRUE,
  min_consensus_count = NULL,
  spatial_id = "barcode_10x"
)
#> filterAirr kept 3718 of 7915 rows (dropped 4197).
```

## Create a SIRUP object

`createSIRUP()` joins the Seurat object and the receptor tables. This
object holds BCRs and TCRs. Give `receptors` a named list with one table
for each receptor type. Each table is a *slot*, and here the slots are
named `"BCR"` and `"TCR"`. Later functions that read receptors take a
`slot` argument. Tell `createSIRUP()` which receptor column holds the
spatial ID and which holds the locus. All slots in the list of receptors
share these field names. You can also specify the image scale and
coordinate settings when constructing the object, which are discussed
further below.

``` r
sirup <- createSIRUP(
  spatial = thymus,
  receptors = list(BCR = bcrs, TCR = tcrs),
  spatial_id = "barcode_10x",
  locus = "locus",
  image_scale = "lowres",
  swap_coords = FALSE,
  metadata = list(tissue = "MG thymus", section = "slice 2")
)

sirup
#> <SIRUP object>
#> Spatial data:    Seurat, 3,203 spatial IDs, 449 genes, 1 image
#> Receptor data:   2 slots
#>   BCR: 2,189 receptor sequences x 56 columns; 817/888 receptor IDs in spatial data (92.0%)
#>   TCR: 3,718 receptor sequences x 56 columns; 1,433/1,592 receptor IDs in spatial data (90.0%)
#> Spatial ID field: barcode_10x
#> Analyses:        0
```

`receptorSlots()` lists the slot names:

``` r
receptorSlots(sirup)
#> [1] "BCR" "TCR"
```

`summary()` gives the number of spatial IDs, receptors, and matches for
each slot:

``` r
summary(sirup)
#> SIRUP summary
#>   Spatial IDs:      3,203
#>   Receptor records: 5,907
#>   Receptor IDs:     2,480
#>   Matched IDs:      2,250 (90.7%)
#>   Matched records:  5,458
#>   Image scale:      lowres
#>   Swap coords:      FALSE
#>   Stored analyses:  0
#> 
#> Per-sample summary
#> # A tibble: 2 × 8
#>   slot  sample  n_spatial_ids n_receptor_records n_receptor_ids n_matched_ids
#>   <chr> <chr>           <int>              <int>          <int>         <int>
#> 1 BCR   spatial          3203               2189            888           817
#> 2 TCR   spatial          3203               3718           1592          1433
#> # ℹ 2 more variables: n_matched_records <int>, id_match_rate <dbl>
```

If an object holds one receptor table, give `receptors` the table
itself, and you do not need `slot`.
[How the SIRUP object works](sirup-object.md) explains slots.

If a `spatial_id`, `locus`, and/or `clone` column are specified when
constructing the SIRUP object, later functions can find these columns
without including them as arguments.

Two settings control how SIRUP constructs plots over the H&E image:

- `image_scale` is `"lowres"` or `"hires"`. Use the image that the
  Seurat object stores. `Load10X_Spatial()` stores the low-resolution
  image by default, though it can use the high-resolution image if
  specified in the `image.name` argument.
- `swap_coords` swaps the x and y coordinates. Set it to `TRUE` only if
  the spots have the right shape but sit rotated or mirrored over the
  image, because the object stores the coordinates as (row, column)
  instead of (x, y). This is easiest to determine by plotting the spots
  as shown below.

The coordinates are generally in pixel space, where `y` counts down from
the top of the image, so when we check we should plot `y` as `-y`. If
the spots then look like the tissue as they do here, keep
`swap_coords = FALSE`.

``` r
coords <- SeuratObject::GetTissueCoordinates(thymus)
ggplot(coords, aes(x, -y)) + geom_point()
```

![](get-started_files/figure-gfm/check-swapcoords-1.jpeg)

If both arguments are included when constructing the SIRUP object, they
will be stored in the object, and plotting functions will automatically
use them. If they are not specified when constructing the SIRUP object,
both settings should be passed to any plotting functions.

<div markdown="1"
style="background: #F7E5BC; padding: 12px; margin-bottom: 24px; line-height: 24px;">

<p style="margin: -12px -12px 12px; padding: 6px 12px; background: #d6b676; color: #ffffff; font-weight: 700;">

<b>Note</b>
</p>

[How the SIRUP object works](sirup-object.md) discusses the SIRUP object
in more detail.

</div>

## Building clones in the SIRUP object

A clone is a group of cells that descend from a common ancestor. Many
SIRUP functions work with clone-level data, but SIRUP does not itself
build clones. The `updateReceptors()` function is a method that can runs
any function on the receptor table and updates the receptor table in the
object with the result. This call runs `hierarchicalClones()` from the
`scoper` package on the BCR slot.

``` r
sirup <- updateReceptors(
  sirup,
  scoper::hierarchicalClones,
  slot = "BCR",
  threshold = 0.1,
  summarize_clones = FALSE,
  nproc = 1
)
#> Warning in prepare_db(db = db, junction = junction, v_call = v_call, j_call =
#> j_call, : Removed 84 sequences with non ATCG characters.
sirup
#> <SIRUP object>
#> Spatial data:    Seurat, 3,203 spatial IDs, 449 genes, 1 image
#> Receptor data:   2 slots
#>   BCR: 2,105 receptor sequences x 57 columns; 797/868 receptor IDs in spatial data (91.8%)
#>   TCR: 3,718 receptor sequences x 56 columns; 1,433/1,592 receptor IDs in spatial data (90.0%)
#> Spatial ID field: barcode_10x
#> Clone ID field:  clone_id
#> Analyses:        0
```

The receptor table now has a `clone_id` column, and SIRUP records it as
the clone field in the object automatically.

## Plot gene expression and receptors on the tissue

`spatialExpressionPlot()` plots gene expression over the H&E image. By
default, it hides spots with zero expression to help the tissue stay
visible, though this can be turned off by setting `zero_tol = -Inf`.

The example object has two assays: `Spatial` (counts and log-normalized
data) and `alra` (ALRA-imputed values), which can help improve
visualization. *AICDA* is a marker for germinal center B cells, and it
is plotted below.

``` r
spatialExpressionPlot(
  sirup,
  features = "AICDA",
  assay = "alra",
  layer = "data",
  title = "AICDA",
  zero_tol = 0,
  point_alpha = 0.8,
  point_size = 1.2
)
```

![](get-started_files/figure-gfm/expression-1.jpeg)

`plotReceptors()` plots all spots that have a receptor. The `group`
argument is the receptor column that determines the color. All BCRs here
are IGH, so they all are colored the same.

``` r
plotReceptors(
  sirup,
  slot = "BCR",
  group = "locus",
  colors = "white",
  receptor_size = 1.2,
  title = "BCR-positive spots"
)
```

![](get-started_files/figure-gfm/receptors-1.jpeg)

To restrict a receptors plot to a set with only a particular value of
the `group` column, use the `group_val` argument. This plot includes
only the three largest IGH clones.

``` r
top_clones <- getReceptors(sirup, slot = "BCR") %>%
  count(clone_id, sort = TRUE) %>%
  slice_head(n = 3) %>%
  pull(clone_id)
top_clones
#> [1] "34"  "288" "196"

plotReceptors(
  sirup,
  slot = "BCR",
  group = "clone_id",
  group_val = top_clones,
  overlap = "average",
  receptor_size = 1.6,
  title = "Three largest clones"
)
```

![](get-started_files/figure-gfm/clones-1.jpeg)

Because this data was generated with 10X Visium spatial sequencing, each
spot likely contains multiple cells. Resultingly, sequences from
distinct groups may share a spot. By default, `plotReceptors()` gives
the spot a combined label and averages the colors of the two groups. The
`overlap` argument controls this behavior.

`plotReceptorsExpression()` combines the two plots. Spots with gene
expression are filled points. Spots with a receptor have a hollow ring
on top:

``` r
plotReceptorsExpression(
  sirup,
  slot = "BCR",
  group = "locus",
  gene = "AICDA",
  assay = "alra",
  layer = "data",
  colors = "white",
  receptor_size = 1.5,
  feature_size = 2,
  title = "AICDA expression and BCR-positive spots"
)
```

![](get-started_files/figure-gfm/receptors-expression-1.jpeg)

## *In silico* micro-dissection of ROIs

Many spatial questions concern a particular region, such as a germinal
center, a tumor margin, or a lesion. `selectSpatialPolygons()` opens an
app where users can draw polygons over regions of interest using the H&E
image and gene expression (e.g., *AICDA*) or spatial object metadata.

``` r
gc_vertices <- selectSpatialPolygons(
  sirup,
  feature = "AICDA",
  assay = "alra",
  layer = "data",
  plot_image = TRUE,
  save_path = "mg_thymus_slice2_gc_polygons.csv"
)
```

![](figures/polygon-app.jpg)

Click around the edge of a region. Each click snaps to the nearest spot.
**Close polygon** joins the last vertex to the first:

![](figures/polygon-click-1.png)![](figures/polygon-click-2.png)![](figures/polygon-closed.png)

After you click **Done**, the app returns the vertices of every polygon.
It writes them to the CSV file at `save_path` (which can be changed
using the CSV path in the app).

`addPolygons()` attaches polygons to the object. Give it the data frame
from the app (`polygons = gc_vertices`) or the CSV file
(`polygons_path`). SIRUP then determines which polygons, if any, contain
each spot and each receptor. The example data include the annotated eGC
polygons from the SIRUP paper.

``` r
sirup <- addPolygons(
  sirup,
  polygons_path = file.path(extdata, "mg_thymus_slice2_gc_polygons.csv")
)

getPolygons(sirup)
#> # A tibble: 9 × 2
#>   polygon_id vertices        
#>   <chr>      <named list>    
#> 1 1          <tibble [7 × 5]>
#> 2 2          <tibble [4 × 5]>
#> 3 3          <tibble [4 × 5]>
#> 4 4          <tibble [4 × 5]>
#> 5 5          <tibble [6 × 5]>
#> 6 6          <tibble [7 × 5]>
#> 7 7          <tibble [7 × 5]>
#> 8 8          <tibble [4 × 5]>
#> 9 9          <tibble [4 × 5]>

getPolygons(sirup)$vertices[[1]]
#> # A tibble: 7 × 5
#>   spatial_id             x     y image         .sirup_polygon_label
#>   <chr>              <dbl> <dbl> <chr>         <chr>               
#> 1 ATCGACCCAATACAGA-1  300.  327. thymus_slice2 1                   
#> 2 AGTTCCTATTTATGTT-1  307.  327. thymus_slice2 1                   
#> 3 CAGTCTGTATACTGGG-1  310.  320. thymus_slice2 1                   
#> 4 GCGCCGTTCCACGATA-1  307.  314. thymus_slice2 1                   
#> 5 TTATGAATGAAAGGGA-1  300.  314. thymus_slice2 1                   
#> 6 ACATCGATCGTTTACC-1  296.  320. thymus_slice2 1                   
#> 7 ATCGACCCAATACAGA-1  300.  327. thymus_slice2 1
```

Plot the polygons over the H&E image with `plotSpatialPolygons()`.

``` r
plotSpatialPolygons(
  sirup,
  polygon_alpha = 0.3,
  label_outside = TRUE,
  label_offset = 0.02,
  label_color = "white",
  label_leader = FALSE
)
```

![](get-started_files/figure-gfm/plot-spatial-polygons-1.jpeg)

Every receptor table now has a `polygon_id` column. Receptors outside
every polygon get `NA`:

``` r
getReceptors(sirup, slot = "BCR") %>%
  count(polygon_id)
#> # A tibble: 9 × 2
#>   polygon_id     n
#>   <chr>      <int>
#> 1 1             28
#> 2 2             23
#> 3 3             14
#> 4 5             47
#> 5 6              4
#> 6 7             30
#> 7 8              6
#> 8 9              4
#> 9 <NA>        1949
```

## Determine which clones dominate the polygons

`polygonReceptorSummary()` counts the receptors, spots, and clones in
each polygon. It stores the result in the object as an analysis.

``` r
sirup <- polygonReceptorSummary(sirup, slot = "BCR", polygon_id = "polygon_id")
getAnalysis(sirup, "polygon_receptor_summary_BCR")
#> # A tibble: 9 × 5
#>   polygon_id n_receptors n_spatial_ids n_clones top_clone_fraction
#>   <chr>            <int>         <int>    <int>              <dbl>
#> 1 1                   28             6       16              0.143
#> 2 2                   23             3       16              0.174
#> 3 3                   14             3        8              0.286
#> 4 4                    0             0        0             NA    
#> 5 5                   47            12       23              0.128
#> 6 6                    4             4        4              0.25 
#> 7 7                   30             8       12              0.167
#> 8 8                    6             3        4              0.333
#> 9 9                    4             3        4              0.25
```

Clonal dominance measures how much of a region the largest clones fill.
`spatialCloneDominance()` computes the fraction of the receptors in each
polygon that belongs to each clone. `plotSpatialPolygonPies()` draws one
pie chart (or stacked bar chart) for each polygon next to the tissue.

``` r
dominance <- spatialCloneDominance(object = sirup, slot = "BCR")

dominance$dominance %>%
  group_by(polygon) %>%
  slice_max(proportion, n = 1, with_ties = FALSE) %>%
  select(polygon, clone_id, n_receptors, proportion)
#> # A tibble: 8 × 4
#> # Groups:   polygon [8]
#>   polygon clone_id n_receptors proportion
#>   <chr>   <chr>          <dbl>      <dbl>
#> 1 1       928                4      0.143
#> 2 2       381                4      0.174
#> 3 3       196                4      0.286
#> 4 5       810                6      0.128
#> 5 6       136                1      0.25 
#> 6 7       739                5      0.167
#> 7 8       242                2      0.333
#> 8 9       222                1      0.25

pies <- plotSpatialPolygonPies(
  dominance = dominance,
  object = sirup,
  fill = "clone_id",
  top_n = 5
)
pies$page_1
#> Warning: Removed 1 row containing missing values or values outside the scale range
#> (`geom_text()`).
```

![](get-started_files/figure-gfm/dominance-1.jpeg)

The function returns one plot for each page, with six pies on a page.
The `top_n` argument sets how many clones get their own color in each
pie. The grey `Other` slice holds the remaining clones.

[Annotate tissue ROIs and analyze local clonal structure](regions.md) covers ROIs in more detail.

## Save an analysis in a SIRUP object

`setAnalysis()` stores analysis within the SIRUP object. Stored analyses
can be accessed with `getAnalysis()`.

``` r
sirup <- setAnalysis(sirup, "gc_dominance", dominance)
listAnalyses(sirup)
#> [1] "polygon_receptor_summary_BCR" "gc_dominance"

getAnalysis(sirup, "gc_dominance") %>% str(max.level = 1)
#> List of 6
#>  $ dominance         :'data.frame':  87 obs. of  11 variables:
#>  $ region_spatial_ids:'data.frame':  55 obs. of  3 variables:
#>  $ region_coordinates:'data.frame':  55 obs. of  9 variables:
#>  $ region_receptors  :'data.frame':  156 obs. of  78 variables:
#>  $ polygons          :'data.frame':  47 obs. of  4 variables:
#>  $ metadata          :List of 1
#>  - attr(*, "class")= chr [1:2] "sirup_spatial_clone_dominance" "list"
```

The stored result is a list. Its `dominance` item is the table of clone
fractions. The other items hold the spots, coordinates, receptors, and
polygon vertices of each region, and the field names that the function
used.

## Save and read a SIRUP object

`saveSIRUP()` writes the object to one RDS file. `readSIRUP()` reads it
back and validates it.

``` r
path <- file.path(tempdir(), "mg_thymus_slice2_brighter.sirup.rds")
saveSIRUP(sirup, path)
sirup <- readSIRUP(path)
sirup
#> <SIRUP object>
#> Spatial data:    Seurat, 3,203 spatial IDs, 449 genes, 1 image
#> Receptor data:   2 slots
#>   BCR: 2,105 receptor sequences x 67 columns; 797/868 receptor IDs in spatial data (91.8%)
#>   TCR: 3,718 receptor sequences x 66 columns; 1,433/1,592 receptor IDs in spatial data (90.0%)
#> Spatial ID field: barcode_10x
#> Clone ID field:  clone_id
#> Analyses:        2
#> Polygons:        9
```

<!-- source: docs/vignettes/llm-agents.md -->

Use SIRUP with your LLM agent
================

An LLM agent can write and run SIRUP code for you, and it can write
better code when it knows how SIRUP works. SIRUP provides agents with:
\* a packaged skill \* the llms files, which are text and JSON copies of
the documentation.

## How to teach your agent about SIRUP

| Method | What is it? | When to choose this? |
|----|----|----|
| The SIRUP skill | An agent skill | Your agent supports skills. Claude Code, Codex, and Antigravity (and likely others) do. |
| The llms files | Text and JSON copies of the documentation | Your agent does not support skills or you do not wish to use one. |
| The readthedocs pages | The pages of this site | You don’t want to upload files to your agent, and it can browse the web. |

## Install the skill

Agent Skills is an open format created by Anthropic, and it is descrbied
at [agentskills.io](https://agentskills.io). A skill is a folder with a
file named `SKILL.md` that explains how to accomplish a task in a
certain way to an agent. The file starts with a name and a description.
At the start of a session, the agent reads the name and the description
of each installed skill. It reads the rest of the folder only when you
request that it uses the skill.

SIRUP ships its skill inside the R package, in `inst/skills/sirup`,
which is automatically copied into the package folder when you install a
package in R. This puts the skill in your R library, so we need to put
it in a place that your agent will look. For convenience, the
`installSIRUPSkill()` function copies the skill to the appropriate
location for Claude, Codex, and Antigravity agents.

``` r
library(SIRUP)

installSIRUPSkill(agent = "claude")        # Claude Code
installSIRUPSkill(agent = "codex")         # Codex
installSIRUPSkill(agent = "antigravity")   # Antigravity
```

Run the line for your agent. By default, the function installs the skill
in the folder that the agent reads for all your projects.

| `agent`                       | Skill folder for all projects |     |
|-------------------------------|-------------------------------|-----|
| `"claude"` (Claude Code)      | `~/.claude/skills/`           |     |
| `"codex"` (Codex)             | `~/.agents/skills/`           |     |
| `"antigravity"` (Antigravity) | `~/.gemini/config/skills/`    |     |

If you only wish to install a skill for a particular project, use the
`install_dir` argument. Claude agents read `.claude/skills/` in the
project, and Codex and Antigravity agents read `.agents/skills/` in the
project.

``` r
installSIRUPSkill(agent = "claude", install_dir = ".claude/skills")
installSIRUPSkill(agent = "codex", install_dir = ".agents/skills")
installSIRUPSkill(agent = "antigravity", install_dir = ".agents/skills")
```

<div markdown="1"
style="background: #9e584a; padding: 12px; margin-bottom: 24px; line-height: 24px;">

<p style="margin: -12px -12px 12px; padding: 6px 12px; background: #8b3620; color: #ffffff; font-weight: 700;">

<b>WARNING</b>
</p>

These skill locations are correct as of late 2026. Updated architectures
or other agent platforms may change them.

</div>

You can also copy the skill by hand.
`system.file("skills", "sirup", package = "SIRUP")` returns the path of
the skill folder. Copy that folder into the skills folder of your agent.

### Check that your agent sees the skill

Start a new session. Ask the agent which skills it has, and look for
`sirup`. Alternatively use `/skills` in a command line interface to list
all available skills. In the Antigravity editor, open the Customizations
menu in the agent panel. If you add a skill while an agent runs, restart
the agent or reload skills (as with `/reload-skills` for Claude) first
to see the new skill.

### Update the skill

New SIRUP versions automatically keep the skill updated. After you
update SIRUP, run `installSIRUPSkill()` once again. It replaces the old
copy by default.

## Use the llms files instead

The SIRUP repository holds four files specfically for LLMs.

| File             | Content                                                 |
|------------------|---------------------------------------------------------|
| `llms.txt`       | A short Markdown index of the documentation, with links |
| `llms.json`      | The same short index in JSON                            |
| `llms-full.txt`  | The whole set of documentation in one text file         |
| `llms-full.json` | The whole set of documentation in JSON                  |

Give an agent that has no skill support the address of `llms.json` or
`llms.txt`. Tell it to read the index and then to fetch the page that it
needs. The full files are large, about 400 KB each, so chat windows may
not be able to hold them. We recommend that you start with the short
index.

## Example requests

Use these requests with the skill installed. Replace the file names with
your own.

``` text
I have a Seurat object in `spatial.rds` and a corresponding spatial AIRR rearrangement in `bcr.tsv.gz`.
Please build a SIRUP object and then build clones. Tell me how many sequences you removed and why.

Which spatial statistic should I use to test whether one clone stays in one place?

Load the region polygons in polygons.csv. Which clones dominate each region?

Build lineage trees for the three largest clones in region 5. Tell me what the run needs
before you start.

Write a Slurm script that runs `processSpatialSample()` on my demultiplexed reads.

This error came from `createSIRUP()`: <paste the error>. Can you please explain it and fix the call?
```

## Work with an agent with care

- **Read the code before you run it.** Ask the agent to explain each
  step.
- **Protect private data.** A hosted agent sends your requests, and the
  files that it reads, to its provider. Check your data agreement before
  you share patient data. The example data that comes with SIRUP is for
  tutorials.
- **Ask for checks.** Ask the agent to print the receptor count before
  and after each change, and to run `validateSIRUP()`.
- **Ask what the agent did not run.** An agent can describe a result
  that it did not produce.
- **Agents cannot draw ROIs.** Unless you give your agent a skill that
  allows it to click, you will have to draw regions with the polygon
  selection RShiny app. These can be subjective at times, so we
  recommend not passing this task to an agent.

**An agent does not replace an expert review of your results.**

## Next steps

- To build a SIRUP object and run a few simple analyses, see
  [Get started with SIRUP](get-started.md).
- To learn more about the structure of the SIRUP object see
  [How the SIRUP object works](sirup-object.md).
- To test spatial patterns, read
  [Choose the right spatial statistic for your question](choose-spatial-statistic.md).

<!-- source: docs/vignettes/multisample.md -->

Analyze multiple spatial sections and bulk BCR-seq
================

<div markdown="1"
style="background: #F7E5BC; padding: 12px; margin-bottom: 24px; line-height: 24px;">

<p style="margin: -12px -12px 12px; padding: 6px 12px; background: #d6b676; color: #ffffff; font-weight: 700;">

<b>Note</b>
</p>

**Time:** ~15 minutes.<br> **Data:** example spatial MG thymus sections,
bulk thymus BCR-seq, and bulk blood BCR-seq.<br>

</div>

Many studies have multiple spatial samples of the same tissue sections,
or multi-modal AIRR-seq from the same patient. Here, we will build and
analyze a single SIRUP object that contains two spatial sections, bulk
thymus BCR-seq, and bulk blood BCR-seq.

The SIRUP object contains \* `spatial`, a named list of spatial Seurat
objects, one for each section. \* `receptors`, a named list of receptor
tables, have one for each type of receptor. One table can hold all BCRs,
including both spatial and bulk data. A `sample` column tells SIRUP
which sample each row belongs to. \* Rows whose `sample` does not name a
section stay in the table as non-spatial rows. SIRUP does not put them
on a tissue, but clone calling, trees, and custom summaries can use
them.

This page follows Figure 5 of the SIRUP paper. The MG thymus data come
from a patient who had a thymectomy. Besides the two Visium sections,
there is bulk BCR-seq of the thymus and bulk BCR-seq of blood, taken at
the thymectomy and 12 months later. The question is which clones in
ectopic germinal centers (eGCs) also appear in the blood. An eGC is a
site in the thymus where B cells proliferate and mutate their receptors.

<div markdown="1"
style="background: #F7E5BC; padding: 12px; margin-bottom: 24px; line-height: 24px;">

<p style="margin: -12px -12px 12px; padding: 6px 12px; background: #d6b676; color: #ffffff; font-weight: 700;">

<b>Note</b>
</p>

This page assumes a basic knowledge of the SIRUP object. To learn how an
object is built, see [Get started with SIRUP](get-started.md). To
learn how the object works, see
[How the SIRUP object works](sirup-object.md).

</div>

## Get the example data

This page uses example files that are slightly too big to be part of the
SIRUP package. This code downloads them. Change `dest` to a folder you
want to keep. The function skips files that are already there.

``` r
extdata <- SIRUP::downloadSIRUPExample(
  dest = file.path(tempdir(), "SIRUP_example"),
  files = c(
    "mg_thymus_slice1_spatial_brighter.rds",
    "mg_thymus_slice2_spatial_brighter.rds",
    "mg_thymus_slice1_bcr.tsv.gz",
    "mg_thymus_slice2_bcr.tsv.gz",
    "mg_thymus_slice2_tcr.tsv.gz",
    "mg_thymus_slice1_gc_polygons.csv",
    "mg_thymus_slice2_gc_polygons.csv",
    "mg_thymus_bulk_thymus_1.tsv.gz",
    "mg_thymus_bulk_thymus_2.tsv.gz",
    "mg_thymus_bulk_blood_month0_1.tsv.gz",
    "mg_thymus_bulk_blood_month0_2.tsv.gz",
    "mg_thymus_bulk_blood_month12_1.tsv.gz",
    "mg_thymus_bulk_blood_month12_2.tsv.gz"
  )
)
#> ℹ Downloading 'mg_thymus_slice1_spatial_brighter.rds'
#> ℹ 'mg_thymus_slice2_spatial_brighter.rds' is already in '/scratch/f007p0j/RtmpscrZTE/SIRUP_example'.
#> ℹ Downloading 'mg_thymus_slice1_bcr.tsv.gz'
#> ℹ 'mg_thymus_slice2_bcr.tsv.gz' is already in '/scratch/f007p0j/RtmpscrZTE/SIRUP_example'.
#> ℹ 'mg_thymus_slice2_tcr.tsv.gz' is already in '/scratch/f007p0j/RtmpscrZTE/SIRUP_example'.
#> ℹ Downloading 'mg_thymus_slice1_gc_polygons.csv'
#> ℹ 'mg_thymus_slice2_gc_polygons.csv' is already in '/scratch/f007p0j/RtmpscrZTE/SIRUP_example'.
#> ℹ Downloading 'mg_thymus_bulk_thymus_1.tsv.gz'
#> ℹ Downloading 'mg_thymus_bulk_thymus_2.tsv.gz'
#> ℹ Downloading 'mg_thymus_bulk_blood_month0_1.tsv.gz'
#> ℹ Downloading 'mg_thymus_bulk_blood_month0_2.tsv.gz'
#> ℹ Downloading 'mg_thymus_bulk_blood_month12_1.tsv.gz'
#> ℹ Downloading 'mg_thymus_bulk_blood_month12_2.tsv.gz'
```

## Load the samples

``` r
library(SIRUP)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
```

Load the two spatial Seurat objects and all of the BCR data.

``` r
spatial <- list(
  mg_thymus_slice1 = readRDS(file.path(extdata, "mg_thymus_slice1_spatial_brighter.rds")),
  mg_thymus_slice2 = readRDS(file.path(extdata, "mg_thymus_slice2_spatial_brighter.rds"))
)

# One AIRR file for each sample, with the compartment that the sample came from
bcr_files <- c(
  mg_thymus_slice1 = "mg_thymus_slice1_bcr.tsv.gz",
  mg_thymus_slice2 = "mg_thymus_slice2_bcr.tsv.gz",
  bulk_thymus_1 = "mg_thymus_bulk_thymus_1.tsv.gz",
  bulk_thymus_2 = "mg_thymus_bulk_thymus_2.tsv.gz",
  bulk_blood_month0_1 = "mg_thymus_bulk_blood_month0_1.tsv.gz",
  bulk_blood_month0_2 = "mg_thymus_bulk_blood_month0_2.tsv.gz",
  bulk_blood_month12_1 = "mg_thymus_bulk_blood_month12_1.tsv.gz",
  bulk_blood_month12_2 = "mg_thymus_bulk_blood_month12_2.tsv.gz"
)
compartments <- c(
  mg_thymus_slice1 = "thymus_slice1",
  mg_thymus_slice2 = "thymus_slice2",
  bulk_thymus_1 = "bulk_thymus",
  bulk_thymus_2 = "bulk_thymus",
  bulk_blood_month0_1 = "blood_month0",
  bulk_blood_month0_2 = "blood_month0",
  bulk_blood_month12_1 = "blood_month12",
  bulk_blood_month12_2 = "blood_month12"
)

bcr_list <- lapply(file.path(extdata, bcr_files), airr::read_rearrangement)
names(bcr_list) <- names(bcr_files)

# Put all BCRs together
all_bcrs <- bind_rows(bcr_list, .id = "sample") %>%
  mutate(compartment = unname(compartments[sample]))
```

Then add the spatial IDs to the spatial BCRs and filter the BCRs to only
include sequences that are productive and have reasonable looking Vs,
Js, and junctions.

``` r
# Add a spatial id to the spatial data
spatial_bcrs <- all_bcrs %>%
  filter(compartment %in% c("thymus_slice1", "thymus_slice2")) %>%
  extractSpatialIds(
    id = "sequence_id",
    spatial_id = "barcode_10x",
    regex = ",([ACGT]{16})$",
    suffix = "-1"
  )
bulk <- all_bcrs %>%
  filter(!compartment %in% c("thymus_slice1", "thymus_slice2"))

bcrs <- bind_rows(spatial_bcrs, bulk) %>%
  mutate(sequence_id = paste(sample, gsub(",", "_", sequence_id), sep = "_")) %>%
  filterAirr(
    locus_val = "IGH",
    min_v_length = 250,
    min_j_length = 30,
    min_junction_length = 10,
    productive_only = TRUE,
    min_consensus_count = NULL
  ) %>%
  filter(!grepl("[^ACGT]", junction))
#> filterAirr kept 5733 of 8849 rows (dropped 3116).

count(bcrs, compartment, sample)
#> # A tibble: 8 × 3
#>   compartment   sample                   n
#>   <chr>         <chr>                <int>
#> 1 blood_month0  bulk_blood_month0_1    182
#> 2 blood_month0  bulk_blood_month0_2    182
#> 3 blood_month12 bulk_blood_month12_1   241
#> 4 blood_month12 bulk_blood_month12_2   108
#> 5 bulk_thymus   bulk_thymus_1          176
#> 6 bulk_thymus   bulk_thymus_2          576
#> 7 thymus_slice1 mg_thymus_slice1      1967
#> 8 thymus_slice2 mg_thymus_slice2      2105
```

Load in and filter TCRs.

``` r
tcrs <- airr::read_rearrangement(file.path(extdata, "mg_thymus_slice2_tcr.tsv.gz")) %>%
  mutate(sample = "mg_thymus_slice2", compartment = "thymus_slice2") %>%
  extractSpatialIds(
    id = "sequence_id",
    spatial_id = "barcode_10x",
    regex = ",([ACGT]{16})$",
    suffix = "-1"
  ) %>%
  mutate(sequence_id = paste(sample, gsub(",", "_", sequence_id), sep = "_")) %>%
  filterAirr(
    locus_val = "TRB",
    min_v_length = 250,
    min_j_length = 30,
    min_junction_length = 10,
    productive_only = TRUE,
    min_consensus_count = NULL
  ) %>%
  filter(!grepl("[^ACGT]", junction))
#> filterAirr kept 3718 of 7915 rows (dropped 4197).
```

We add columns `sample` and `compartment` to each AIRR table. We extract
the barcodes from the spatial sequences and then filter., Make sure the
`sequence_id`s are unique. The code adds the sample name in front of the
`sequence_id`, because IDs may repeat between datasets, and it replaces
the comma with `_`, because dowser renames tree tips that contain a
comma.

The section rows get a `sample` that matches the names of the `spatial`
list. The bulk and blood rows have their own sample names and no
barcode.

<div markdown="1"
style="background: #9e584a; padding: 12px; margin-bottom: 24px; line-height: 24px;">

<p style="margin: -12px -12px 12px; padding: 6px 12px; background: #8b3620; color: #ffffff; font-weight: 700;">

<b>WARNING</b>
</p>

Make sure that the `sample` column of the receptor tables matches the
names of the `spatial` list for the spatial receptor sequences. Also
make sure that the `sequence_id` column is (1) unique across all
samples, and (2) does not contain commas to avoid problems with Dowser.

</div>

## Create a multi-sample SIRUP object

Pass `createSIRUP()` the named list of Seurat objects, and pass
`receptors` a named list of receptor tables. The tables are the slots
`"BCR"` and `"TCR"`, and only the spatial section has TCRs. Pass the
name of the `sample` column to `sample_id`. All slots use this column.

``` r
sirup <- createSIRUP(
  spatial = spatial,
  receptors = list(BCR = bcrs, TCR = tcrs),
  spatial_id = "barcode_10x",
  sample_id = "sample",
  image_scale = "lowres",
  swap_coords = FALSE
)

sirup
#> <SIRUP object>
#> Spatial data:    Seurat, 6,599 spatial IDs, 449 genes, 2 spatial samples, 2 images
#> Receptor data:   2 slots
#>   BCR: 5,537 receptor sequences x 58 columns; 1,567/1,640 receptor IDs in spatial data (95.5%)
#>   TCR: 3,610 receptor sequences x 58 columns; 1,414/1,571 receptor IDs in spatial data (90.0%)
#> Samples:         2
#> Spatial ID field: barcode_10x
#> Sample ID field: sample
#> Analyses:        0
spatialSamples(sirup) # Get the names of the spatial samples
#> [1] "mg_thymus_slice1" "mg_thymus_slice2"
```

Visium barcodes repeat between sections, e.g., `AAACAAGTATCTCCCA-1`
exists in both. SIRUP matches each receptor to a spot by sample and
barcode, so the two sections stay separate.

If the sections need different image settings, give named values:
`image_scale = c(mg_thymus_slice1 = "hires", mg_thymus_slice2 = "lowres")`.

## Get one sample

The accessors (`getReceptors` and `getSpatial`) take a `sample_id`
argument, and the receptor accessors also take a `slot` argument.

``` r
getSpatial(sirup, "mg_thymus_slice1")
#> An object of class Seurat 
#> 506 features across 3396 samples within 2 assays 
#> Active assay: Spatial (449 features, 0 variable features)
#>  2 layers present: counts, data
#>  1 other assay present: alra
#>  1 spatial field of view present: thymus_slice1
nrow(getReceptors(sirup, "mg_thymus_slice1", slot = "BCR"))
#> [1] 1967
nrow(getReceptors(sirup, slot = "BCR"))
#> [1] 5537
```

`subsetSIRUP()` returns a new SIRUP object with only data that matches
the named sample, which here is `mg_thymus_slice1`. The new object has
only the spatial GEX data from the entry in the `spatial` list named
`mg_thymus_slice1`, and only the BCRs that have
`sample == "mg_thymus_slice1"`.

``` r
slice1 <- subsetSIRUP(sirup, sample_id = "mg_thymus_slice1")
slice1
#> <SIRUP object>
#> Spatial data:    Seurat, 3,396 spatial IDs, 449 genes, 1 image
#> Receptor data:   2 slots
#>   BCR: 1,967 receptor sequences x 58 columns; 770/772 receptor IDs in spatial data (99.7%)
#>   TCR: 0 receptor sequences x 58 columns; 0/0 receptor IDs in spatial data (NaN%)
#> Spatial ID field: barcode_10x
#> Analyses:        0
```

`mergeSIRUP()` goes the other way. It combines single-section objects
into a multi-sample object, and it adds a sample column with the names
that are given.

``` r
slice2 <- subsetSIRUP(sirup, sample_id = "mg_thymus_slice2")
merged <- mergeSIRUP(
  slice1, slice2,
  samples = c("mg_thymus_slice1", "mg_thymus_slice2"),
  sample_field = "sample"
)
merged
#> <SIRUP object>
#> Spatial data:    Seurat, 6,599 spatial IDs, 449 genes, 2 spatial samples, 2 images
#> Receptor data:   2 slots
#>   BCR: 4,072 receptor sequences x 58 columns; 1,567/1,640 receptor IDs in spatial data (95.5%)
#>   TCR: 3,610 receptor sequences x 58 columns; 1,414/1,571 receptor IDs in spatial data (90.0%)
#> Samples:         2
#> Spatial ID field: barcode_10x
#> Sample ID field: sample
#> Analyses:        0
```

## Add ROI polygons for each section

As discussed in [Annotate tissue ROIs and analyze local clonal structure](regions.md), we can add ROI
polygons to the SIRUP object with `addPolygons()`. Since we have
multiple spatial samples, we pass a named (with the section names)
vector of polygon files.

``` r
sirup <- addPolygons(sirup, polygons_path = c(
  mg_thymus_slice1 = file.path(extdata, "mg_thymus_slice1_gc_polygons.csv"),
  mg_thymus_slice2 = file.path(extdata, "mg_thymus_slice2_gc_polygons.csv")
))

getPolygons(sirup)
#> # A tibble: 19 × 3
#>    polygon_id           sample           vertices        
#>    <chr>                <chr>            <named list>    
#>  1 mg_thymus_slice1::1  mg_thymus_slice1 <tibble [6 × 6]>
#>  2 mg_thymus_slice1::10 mg_thymus_slice1 <tibble [6 × 6]>
#>  3 mg_thymus_slice1::2  mg_thymus_slice1 <tibble [4 × 6]>
#>  4 mg_thymus_slice1::3  mg_thymus_slice1 <tibble [5 × 6]>
#>  5 mg_thymus_slice1::4  mg_thymus_slice1 <tibble [5 × 6]>
#>  6 mg_thymus_slice1::5  mg_thymus_slice1 <tibble [6 × 6]>
#>  7 mg_thymus_slice1::6  mg_thymus_slice1 <tibble [8 × 6]>
#>  8 mg_thymus_slice1::7  mg_thymus_slice1 <tibble [5 × 6]>

#> 10 mg_thymus_slice1::9  mg_thymus_slice1 <tibble [5 × 6]>
#> 11 mg_thymus_slice2::1  mg_thymus_slice2 <tibble [7 × 6]>
#> 12 mg_thymus_slice2::2  mg_thymus_slice2 <tibble [4 × 6]>
#> 13 mg_thymus_slice2::3  mg_thymus_slice2 <tibble [4 × 6]>
#> 14 mg_thymus_slice2::4  mg_thymus_slice2 <tibble [4 × 6]>
#> 15 mg_thymus_slice2::5  mg_thymus_slice2 <tibble [6 × 6]>
#> 16 mg_thymus_slice2::6  mg_thymus_slice2 <tibble [7 × 6]>
#> 17 mg_thymus_slice2::7  mg_thymus_slice2 <tibble [7 × 6]>
#> 18 mg_thymus_slice2::8  mg_thymus_slice2 <tibble [4 × 6]>
#> 19 mg_thymus_slice2::9  mg_thymus_slice2 <tibble [4 × 6]>
```

Both files number their polygons from 1, so SIRUP adds the sample ID to
each polygon ID, i.e., `mg_thymus_slice1::1` and `mg_thymus_slice2::1`.

## Plot multiple spatial sections

Functions that create spatial plots for a multi-sample object return a
list with one plot for each section. Set `combine_sample_plots = TRUE`
to get one combined figure, or pass `sample_id` to plot one section.

``` r
spatialExpressionPlot(
  sirup,
  features = "AICDA",
  assay = "alra",
  layer = "data",
  title = c("AICDA, section 1", "AICDA, section 2"),
  point_size = 1.5,
  combine_sample_plots = TRUE
)
```

![](multisample_files/figure-gfm/plots-1.jpeg)

``` r
spatialExpressionPlot(
  sirup,
  features = "AICDA",
  assay = "alra",
```

## Infer clones and trees across all samples

Infer clones for the entire set of BCRs, including both spatial and bulk
datasets, using `updateReceptors()` with `scoper::hierarchicalClones()`.
Clones represent the set of B cells that are inferred to descend from a
common ancestor.

``` r
sirup <- updateReceptors(
  sirup,
  scoper::hierarchicalClones,
  slot = "BCR",
  threshold = 0.1,
  summarize_clones = FALSE,
  nproc = 1
)
```

Phylogenetic trees show the evolutionary history of a clone. Each tip in
the tree is one observed sequence. With SIRUP, trees can include tips
from all spatial and bulk samples.

This guide uses clone 1045. It has sequences in spatial section 2,
including ectopic germinal center (eGC) 5, in the bulk thymus, and in
the blood at both time points.

``` r
tree_clone <- "1045"
tree_section <- "mg_thymus_slice2"

getReceptors(sirup, slot = "BCR") %>%
  filter(clone_id == tree_clone) %>%
  count(compartment)
#> # A tibble: 4 × 2
#>   compartment       n
#>   <chr>         <int>
#> 1 blood_month0     15
#> 2 blood_month12     4
#> 3 bulk_thymus      10
#> 4 thymus_slice2    15
```

Next, make the germline of the clone with `dowser::createGermlines()`.
The germline is the sequence of the unmutated common ancestor, which
roots the tree. As in [Infer clones and lineage trees in situ](clones-and-trees.md),
building the germline requires IMGT references. Set the variable
`imgt_dir` to the folder that contains them.

<div markdown="1"
style="background: #F7E5BC; padding: 12px; margin-bottom: 24px; line-height: 24px;">

<p style="margin: -12px -12px 12px; padding: 6px 12px; background: #d6b676; color: #ffffff; font-weight: 700;">

<b>Note</b>
</p>

If you have not yet set up the IMGT references, see the
[documentation](https://github.com/hoehnlab/airrblast) for the
`airrblast` package and download and set up the IMGT references.

</div>

Keep `compartment` in `traits`, because the tree plot uses it to set the
tip shapes.

``` r
tree_sirup <- updateReceptors(sirup, dplyr::filter, clone_id == tree_clone, slot = "BCR")
tree_sirup <- updateReceptors(
  tree_sirup,
  dowser::createGermlines,
  slot = "BCR",
  references = dowser::readIMGT(imgt_dir),
  id = "sequence_id"
)
#> Warning in fun(sirup_data, ...): 107 sequence lengths longer than predicted
#> germlines, consider setting trim_lengths=TRUE if germlines fail
#> [1] "Read in 1198 from 17 fasta files"
```

To build trees with Dowser, we need a formatted clones object.
`formatSpatialClones()` wraps `dowser::formatClones()` but allows users
to provide a SIRUP object, and it automatically places a
`formatted_clones` object in the SIRUP object’s analysis slot. Then, we
can call `getSpatialTrees()`, which wraps `dowser::getTrees()` but
allows users to provide a SIRUP object, and puts the trees in the SIRUP
object’s analysis slot.

``` r
tree_sirup <- formatSpatialClones(
  tree_sirup,
  slot = "BCR",
  id = "sequence_id",
  traits = c("barcode_10x", "sample", "compartment", "polygon_id")
)

tree_sirup <- getSpatialTrees(tree_sirup, slot = "BCR")
trees <- getAnalysis(tree_sirup, "trees_BCR")
```

`plotSpatialCloneTreePairs()` plots the tree on the left and the H&E
image of the section(s) on the right. Tips in the tree are plotted in
their corresponding spots in the tissue if they are from the spatial
data. The argument `shape_by` sets the shape for each tip according to
the provided column (here `"compartment"`), and `color_by` colors the
tips by cluster. `clusterTreesTips()` clusters the tips in the tree by
genetic relationships in order to provide visual clarity for paired
plots. Here, `k = 6` splits the tree into six groups of tips.

``` r
trees <- clusterTreesTips(trees, k = 6, id = "sequence_id", method = "monophyletic_clades")

pair <- plotSpatialCloneTreePairs(
  trees,
  object = sirup,
  slot = "BCR",
  id = "sequence_id",
  color_by = "tree_cluster",
  shape_by = "compartment",
  shape_values = c(
    thymus_slice1 = 21, thymus_slice2 = 21, bulk_thymus = 22,
    blood_month0 = 24, blood_month12 = 23
  ),
  polygons = TRUE,
  polygon_alpha = 0,
  polygon_color = "black",
  show_spatial_legend = TRUE,
  legend_theme = ggplot2::theme(
    legend.text = ggplot2::element_text(size = 7),
    legend.title = ggplot2::element_text(size = 8, face = "bold"),
    legend.key.size = grid::unit(0.3, "cm")
  )
)

names(pair)
#> [1] "1045"
```

In general, the `plotSpatialCloneTreePairs()` function returns a list of
plots, one for each clone. If a clone has sequences in multiple spatial
samples, the list will have one element for each clone-sample
combination, named `<clone>::<sample>`. Each one pairs the full tree
with the map of one section. The code below shows the section that holds
the eGC tips.

``` r
key <- paste0(tree_clone, "::", tree_section)
if (!key %in% names(pair)) key <- tree_clone
section_pair <- pair[[key]]

section_pair
```

![](multisample_files/figure-gfm/tree-plot-show-1.jpeg)

## Save and read the object

`saveSIRUP()` writes the object to a file. `readSIRUP()` reads it back
and checks its structure.

``` r
path <- file.path(tempdir(), "mg_thymus.sirup.rds")
saveSIRUP(sirup, path)
readSIRUP(path)
#> <SIRUP object>
#> Spatial data:    Seurat, 6,599 spatial IDs, 449 genes, 2 spatial samples, 2 images
#> Receptor data:   2 slots
#>   BCR: 5,537 receptor sequences x 79 columns; 1,567/1,640 receptor IDs in spatial data (95.5%)
#>   TCR: 3,610 receptor sequences x 68 columns; 1,414/1,571 receptor IDs in spatial data (90.0%)
#> Samples:         2
#> Spatial ID field: barcode_10x
#> Sample ID field: sample
#> Clone ID field:  clone_id
#> Analyses:        0
#> Polygons:        19
```
