<!-- source: docs/vignettes/processing.md -->

Process demultiplexed reads
================

<div markdown="1"
style="background: #F7E5BC; padding: 12px; margin-bottom: 24px; line-height: 24px;">

<p style="margin: -12px -12px 12px; padding: 6px 12px; background: #d6b676; color: #ffffff; font-weight: 700;">

<b>Note</b>
</p>

**Time:** ~30 minutes.<br> **Data:** example MG thymus read-level data
in SIRUP.

</div>

Here, we will take demultiplexed long-read sequences and process them
into an [AIRR
rearrangement](https://docs.airr-community.org/en/latest/datarep/rearrangements.html).

## Get the example data

This page uses example files that are not part of the SIRUP package.
This code downloads them. Change `dest` to a folder you want to keep.
The default folder is temporary. The function skips files that are
already there.

``` r
extdata <- SIRUP::downloadSIRUPExample(
  dest = file.path(tempdir(), "SIRUP_example"),
  files = c(
  "mg_thymus_slice2_reads.tsv.gz",
  "mg_thymus_slice2_bcr.tsv.gz",
  "mg_thymus_slice2_spatial_brighter.rds"
  )
)
#> ℹ Downloading 'mg_thymus_slice2_reads.tsv.gz'
#> ℹ 'mg_thymus_slice2_bcr.tsv.gz' is already in '/scratch/f007p0j/RtmpscrZTE/SIRUP_example'.
#> ℹ 'mg_thymus_slice2_spatial_brighter.rds' is already in '/scratch/f007p0j/RtmpscrZTE/SIRUP_example'.
```

## Demultiplexing long-read sequences

SIRUP does not demultiplex long-read sequencing data on its own. At
present, users should demultiplex their data with

1.  RAD, the read-structure agnostic demultiplexer, which can be used
    [via the command line](https://github.com/indianewok/rad) or
    [natively in R](https://github.com/indianewok/rrad). SIRUP can then
    process the demultiplexed long-reads.
2.  [LongAIRR](https://github.com/AGImkeller/LongAIRR), which
    demultiplexes and processes long-read sequencing data.

If using LongAIRR, the output is an AIRR rearrangement that can be used
directly, without further processing in SIRUP. In this case, the rest of
this vignette is not needed.

## SIRUP processing pipeline

Spatial AIRR-seq libraries are sets of long-read sequences of B and T
cell receptor transcripts. Each read carries a spatial ID (or barcode),
which is a short DNA tag that identifies the spot where the molecule
came from. Many protocols also include a UMI (unique molecular
identifier), a tag that identifies the original molecule.

Processing in SIRUP is done with the `processSpatialSample()` function.
It consists of the following steps.

|  | Step | What it does |
|----|----|----|
| 1 | IgBLAST (`airrblast::assignGenes()`) | Annotates each read with V(D)J genes |
| 2 | `filterAirr()` | Removes reads that are not receptors or are too short to use |
| 3 | `ClusterSets.py` (pRESTO) | Groups the reads of each spot by sequence identity (using vsearch) |
| 4 | `AlignSets.py` (pRESTO) | Aligns the reads in each group (using MUSCLE) |
| 5 | `BuildConsensus.py` (pRESTO) | Builds one consensus sequence per group |
| 6 | `airrblast::assignGenes()` and `airrblast::addGaps()` | Annotates the consensus sequences, adds the IMGT gaps, and writes the AIRR table |

Long-read sequencing has a high error rate. A consensus of several reads
removes most random errors. The spot barcode stays in the sequence
header through every step, so each consensus sequence keeps its spot.

## Install and set up dependencies

### IgBLAST and IMGT germline references

See more detailed instructions in the [airrblast
documentation](https://github.com/hoehnlab/airrblast/tree/main).

Briefly, download and decompress
[IgBLAST](https://ftp.ncbi.nih.gov/blast/executables/igblast/release/LATEST/).

<div markdown="1"
style="background: #9e584a; padding: 12px; margin-bottom: 24px; line-height: 24px;">

<p style="margin: -12px -12px 12px; padding: 6px 12px; background: #8b3620; color: #ffffff; font-weight: 700;">

<b>WARNING</b>
</p>

There is a patch to the latest stable release of IgBLAST. Download the
patched .aux files
[here](https://ftp.ncbi.nih.gov/blast/executables/igblast/release/patch/)
(in `optional_file`). Then swap them into your `optional_file` directory
in your IgBLAST installation.

</div>

Then download the IMGT germline references and set up the IgBLAST
database with `airrblast`. airrblast supports human, mouse, and rhesus
macaque.

``` r
library(airrblast)
library(airr)

# name/location of the uncompressed IgBLAST directory
igblast_dir <- "ncbi-igblast-1.22.0"

# Download IMGT GENE-DB into directory "imgt"
# Do this only once
downloadIMGT("imgt", organism="human", verbose=1)

# Set up search databases for IgBlast using imgt database
# Do this only once
imgtToIgblast("imgt", "igblast", igblast_dir)
```

### Other dependencies

- [**pRESTO**](https://presto.readthedocs.io/en/stable/install.html#installation).
- [**vsearch**](https://github.com/torognes/vsearch).
- [**MUSCLE**](https://www.drive5.com/muscle/downloads_v3.htm) v3.8.31.

<div markdown="1"
style="background: #F7E5BC; padding: 12px; margin-bottom: 24px; line-height: 24px;">

<p style="margin: -12px -12px 12px; padding: 6px 12px; background: #d6b676; color: #ffffff; font-weight: 700;">

<b>Note</b>
</p>

Paths such as `~/share/igblast` and `~/bin/muscle3.8.31_i86linux64` in
this page are examples. Replace them with the paths on your system.

</div>

Check that R can find the programs. This chunk shows code only:

``` r
Sys.which(c(
  "ClusterSets.py", "ParseHeaders.py", "AlignSets.py", "BuildConsensus.py",
  "vsearch"
))
file.exists(file.path("~/share/igblast", "bin", "igblastn"))
```

An empty string means R cannot find that program. Add its folder to
`PATH`, or give its full path to `processSpatialSample()`
(`muscle_exec`). SIRUP runs IgBLAST through airrblast. It uses
`<igblast_base>/bin/igblastn`.

## Process the demultiplexed reads

To go from demultiplexed reads to an AIRR table, give the FASTA file to
`processSpatialSample()`. It runs IgBLAST on each read, reads the
barcode and UMI from the header, filters the reads, builds the consensus
sequences, and writes the AIRR table. The rest of *this* section is
optional. Skip ahead to [Run the consensus
pipeline](#run-the-consensus-pipeline) if you do not want to run the
first IgBLAST pass by hand and examine the reads before building
consensus sequences.

### Run the first IgBLAST pass by hand

RAD/rRAD produces a FASTA file with a header that includes each read
holds the spatial ID and the UMI, in the form `id|BARCODE=YYY|UMI=XXX`.
`airrblast::assignGenes()` annotates every read with V(D)J genes and
writes an AIRR table. It works with plain FASTA files only, so make sure
to decompress a gzipped file before running. `parseRadSequenceIds()`
copies the barcode and the UMI from the read ID into `barcode` and `umi`
columns automatically.

This chunk shows code only. It needs IgBLAST and a full-size input:

``` r
library(airrblast)

assignGenes(
  file = "prepared/sample-igblast.fasta",
  igblast = "~/share/igblast",
  refs = "~/share/igblast_refs",
  organism = "human",
  locus = "Ig",
  outfile = "processed/reads_igblast.tsv",
  nproc = 8,
  return = FALSE
)

reads <- airr::read_rearrangement("processed/reads_igblast.tsv")
reads <- parseRadSequenceIds(reads)
```

Use `locus = "TR"` for TCRs. BCRs and TCRs need to run as separate
calls. The metadata must be in the ID, before any white space. If the
header has a different format, use `extractSpatialIds()`.

`reads` is now a read-level AIRR table. The next section examines and
filters such a table. You can also give it to `processSpatialSample()`
with `input_type = "airr"`, as shown in [Run the consensus
pipeline](#run-the-consensus-pipeline).

### Examine and filter demultiplexed reads by hand

As an example, SIRUP includes 2,000 read-level IgBLAST rows from one
section of human thymus. They have the form of the table that the first
IgBLAST pass makes.

``` r
library(dplyr)

reads <- airr::read_rearrangement(
  file.path(extdata, "mg_thymus_slice2_reads.tsv.gz")
)

dim(reads)
#> [1] 2000  130
count(reads, locus, sort = TRUE)
#> # A tibble: 4 × 2
#>   locus     n
#>   <chr> <int>
#> 1 IGH    1259
#> 2 IGL     480
#> 3 IGK     205
#> 4 <NA>     56
```

Many reads are fragments, light chains, or other transcripts.
`filterAirr()` is a function that conveniently filters out low quality
reads and keeps those potentially worth using to build a consensus. We
recommend using the thresholds given below.

``` r
reads$barcode <- reads$cell_barcode

igh_reads <- filterAirr(
  reads,
  locus_val = "IGH",
  min_v_length = 100,
  min_j_length = 10,
  min_junction_length = 1,
  productive_only = FALSE,
  min_consensus_count = NULL,
  spatial_id = "barcode"
)
#> filterAirr kept 750 of 2000 rows (dropped 1250).

spatialReceptorSummary(igh_reads, spatial_id = "barcode")
#> # A tibble: 1 × 4
#>   n_sequences n_spatial_ids n_loci n_productive
#>         <int>         <int>  <int>        <int>
#> 1         750           451      1          307
```

`plotLengthQc()` shows the V, J, and junction lengths. It can be used to
choose the thresholds rather than using the above.

``` r
plotLengthQc(igh_reads, bin_width = 10, title = "IGH reads")
```

![](processing_files/figure-gfm/length-qc-1.jpeg)

## Run the consensus pipeline

`processSpatialSample()` runs every step from the previously shown
table. It will print each command before it runs, so that if a command
fails debugging is straightforward. This section shows code only.

You can start from three types of input. Demultiplexed reads (the first
row) are the usual start:

| `input` | `input_type` | First step that runs |
|----|----|----|
| FASTA or FASTQ from RAD/rRAD | `"auto"` or `"raw_reads"` | IgBLAST on each read |
| AIRR table (path or data frame) from a first IgBLAST pass | `"auto"` or `"airr"` | `filterAirr()` |
| FASTA that is already filtered, with the spot in the header | `"spatial_fasta"` | sequence clustering |

### From demultiplexed reads

This call takes the FASTA from RAD/rRAD all the way to a properly
formatted AIRR rearrangement. It will run the first IgBLAST pass and
filtering. Note that you should replace the paths below with your own
paths.

``` r
result <- processSpatialSample(
  input = "prepared/sample-igblast.fasta",
  output_dir = "processed/bcr",
  receptor = "ig",
  organism = "human",
  igblast_base = "~/share/igblast",
  igblast_refs = "~/share/igblast_refs",
  imgt_dir = "~/share/imgt",
  muscle_exec = "~/bin/muscle3.8.31_i86linux64",
  identity = 1.0,
  consensus_freq = 0.51,
  consensus_min_count = 2,
  nproc = 8
)

result$db_pass
```

The key arguments here are:

| `argument` | `options` | What it does |
|----|----|----|
| `receptor` | `"ig"` or `"tr"` | Assign IG (for BCRs) or TR (for TCRs) genes with IgBLAST |
| `identity` | 0-1 | How closely do sequences have to match within a spatial spot to be clustered together? |
| `consensus_freq` | 0-1 | What proportion of sequences in a cluster must have the same nucleotide at each position for the consensus sequence to not report an N? |
| `consensus_min_count` | `2` | Require at least 2 reads to support a consensus sequence |
| `nproc` | `8` | Use 8 processes for parallel execution |

### Choosing processing settings

These settings are recommended to change depending on the method used to
perform spatial sequencing. Here, this is 10X Visium data, where spatial
spots are 55$\mu$m in diameter and it is reasonable to expect ~10 cells
per spot. As such, we do not know if slight differences in BCR sequences
seen in the same spot are sequencing errors or mutated BCR sequences
from different cells, so we recommend using `identity = 1.0` to be safe.

Since TCRs do not mutate, we recommend a looser identity threshold,
`identity = 0.975` for 10X Visium data.

For other formats of data that have single-cell or near single-cell
resolution, such as Visium HD or Curio Trekker, we recommend using
`identity = 0.95`, as it is not expected that multiple cells would be
present within the same spot.

We recommend `consensus_freq = 0.51` and `consensus_min_count = 2`
regardless of data.

### Using UMI support

If your spatial sequencing data includes UMIs, which the 10X Visium data
here does, you can use UMI support to group reads from the same
molecule. We expect that differences in sequences with identical UMIs
are likely sequencing errors. By setting `umi_support = TRUE`, SIRUP
first groups the reads of each spot and UMI at a looser identity
(`umi_identity`, default 0.95). It builds one consensus per molecule
from productive reads only. Then, the same spot-level clustering step as
discussed above combines the molecules and sums their reads counts.

The point of using UMI support is to let multiple reads within the same
UMI be counted as support for consensus sequence building, rather than
as separate reads.

This call of `processSpatialSample` is what was used in the SIRUP paper
to process the demultiplexed data with UMI support. `filter_args` are
passed to a call of `filterAirr()` that gets run after the first IgBLAST
step to reduce downstream computational time. If you do not pass a set
of `filter_args`, the filtering step is skipped.

``` r
result <- processSpatialSample(
  input = "prepared/sample-igblast.fasta",
  output_dir = "processed/bcr_umi",
  receptor = "ig",
  identity = 1.0,
  consensus_freq = 0.51,
  cluster_field = "barcode",
  igblast_base = "~/share/igblast",
  igblast_refs = "~/share/igblast_refs",
  imgt_dir = "~/share/imgt",
  muscle_exec = "~/bin/muscle3.8.31_i86linux64",
  nproc = 8,
  umi_support = TRUE,
  umi_field = "umi",
  umi_identity = 0.95,
  min_umi_support = 2,
  filter_args = list(
    locus_val = "IGH",
    min_v_length = 100,
    min_j_length = 10,
    productive_only = FALSE,
    complete_vdj = FALSE,
    min_consensus_count = NULL,
    spatial_id = "barcode",
    add_spatial_sequence_id = FALSE
  )
)

result$db_pass_umi
```

With `umi_support = TRUE`, the result has two AIRR tables. `db_pass`
holds every consensus sequence. `db_pass_umi` holds the sequences with
at least `min_umi_support` reads.

### Running multiple samples

`processSpatialSamples()` runs `processSpatialSample()` on each input,
with the same settings.

``` r
processSpatialSamples(
  inputs = c("prepared/slice1.fasta", "prepared/slice2.fasta"),
  output_dirs = c("processed/slice1", "processed/slice2"),
  receptor = "ig",
  igblast_base = "~/share/igblast",
  igblast_refs = "~/share/igblast_refs",
  imgt_dir = "~/share/imgt",
  nproc = 8
)
```

<div markdown="1"
style="background: #F7E5BC; padding: 12px; margin-bottom: 24px; line-height: 24px;">

<p style="margin: -12px -12px 12px; padding: 6px 12px; background: #d6b676; color: #ffffff; font-weight: 700;">

<b>Tip</b>
</p>

On a cluster, submit one job per sample. Each job calls
`processSpatialSample()` once.

</div>

## After `processSpatialSample()`

The pipeline writes the consensus `sequence_id` as
`<cluster>,<barcode>`. The example data include the AIRR rearrangement
of consensus sequences from a thymus section. Read in and examine the
data below.

``` r
consensus <- airr::read_rearrangement(
  file.path(extdata, "mg_thymus_slice2_bcr.tsv.gz")
)
head(consensus$sequence_id)
#> [1] "9,TGATTCCCGGTTACCT"  "11,TGATTCCCGGTTACCT" "2,TGATTCCCGGTTACCT" 
#> [4] "6,TGATTCCCGGTTACCT"  "5,CCTACATTCACAGACG"  "3,CCTACATTCACAGACG"
```

`extractSpatialIds()` copies the part of an ID that a regular expression
matches into a new column. The `suffix` argument adds `-1`, so the
barcode matches the spot names that Space Ranger writes to the spatial
gene expression data.

``` r
consensus <- extractSpatialIds(
  consensus,
  id = "sequence_id", # look in column
  spatial_id = "barcode_10x", # write to column
  regex = ",([ACGT]{16})$", # what to extract
  suffix = "-1" # suffix to add
)
head(consensus$barcode_10x)
#> [1] "TGATTCCCGGTTACCT-1" "TGATTCCCGGTTACCT-1" "TGATTCCCGGTTACCT-1"
#> [4] "TGATTCCCGGTTACCT-1" "CCTACATTCACAGACG-1" "CCTACATTCACAGACG-1"
```

To examine the consensus sequences that pass through
`processSpatialSample()`, we add a few quality
metrics.`addSequenceQualityMetrics()` adds three columns that help you
set thresholds for further filtering. `non_N_nucleotide_prop` (fraction
of nucleotides that are not N), `max_gap_length` ( longest gap in the
alignment), and `opening_gap_length` (length of a gap at the beginning
of the sequence).

``` r
consensus <- addSequenceQualityMetrics(
  consensus,
  sequence = "sequence",
  alignment = "sequence_alignment"
)
summary(consensus[, c("non_N_nucleotide_prop", "max_gap_length", "consensus_count")])
#>  non_N_nucleotide_prop max_gap_length   consensus_count 
#>  Min.   :0.9510        Min.   :  6.00   Min.   : 1.000  
#>  1st Qu.:1.0000        1st Qu.: 12.00   1st Qu.: 1.000  
#>  Median :1.0000        Median : 12.00   Median : 1.000  
#>  Mean   :0.9982        Mean   : 63.71   Mean   : 1.442  
#>  3rd Qu.:1.0000        3rd Qu.:131.00   3rd Qu.: 1.000  
#>  Max.   :1.0000        Max.   :220.00   Max.   :35.000
```

We then recommend filtering the processed data further to ensure
analyses are done on high quality sequences. We recommend keeping
productive sequences with V gene length at least 250 nucleotides, J gene
length at least 30 nucleotides, and junction length at least 10.
Futhermore, we filter such that sequences are not allowed to have a gap
longer than 15 nucleotides for BCRs and 24 nucleotides for TCRs.

We do not pass a minimum consensus count because the table only includes
sequences with at least two reads supporting the consensus.

``` r
bcrs <- filterAirr(
  consensus,
  locus_val = "IGH",
  min_v_length = 250,
  min_j_length = 30,
  min_junction_length = 10,
  productive_only = TRUE,
  min_consensus_count = NULL,
  max_gap_length = 15,
  spatial_id = "barcode_10x"
)
#> filterAirr kept 2073 of 3793 rows (dropped 1720).

nrow(consensus)
#> [1] 3793
nrow(bcrs)
#> [1] 2073
```

The table is now ready for `createSIRUP()`.

Use QuPath annotations to define ROIs
================

<div markdown="1"
style="background: #F7E5BC; padding: 12px; margin-bottom: 24px; line-height: 24px;">

<p style="margin: -12px -12px 12px; padding: 6px 12px; background: #d6b676; color: #ffffff; font-weight: 700;">

<b>Note</b>
</p>

**Time:** ~5 minutes.<br> **Data:** The example SIRUP object and the
QuPath exported GeoJSON polygons file.

</div>

Here, we will add polygons that were drawn in
[QuPath](https://qupath.github.io) to a SIRUP object.

Regions of interest (ROIs), or polygons, can be drawn in SIRUP with
`selectSpatialPolygons()` (see
[Annotate tissue ROIs and analyze local clonal structure](regions.md)). Pathologists often draw ROIs
in QuPath, a free program for working with tissue images. SIRUP can read
exported QuPath polygon annotations (if exported as a GeoJSON) and add
them to a SIRUP object.

## Load the example object

This code downloads a saved SIRUP object for MG thymus section 2, which
is slightly too big to come directly with the package, and the QuPath
exported polygons. Change `dest` to a whatever folder you wish to save
the example data in. To see how the object was built, see
[Get started with SIRUP](get-started.md).

``` r
extdata <- SIRUP::downloadSIRUPExample(
  dest = file.path(tempdir(), "SIRUP_example"),
  files = c(
    "mg_thymus_slice2_brighter.sirup.rds",
    "mg_thymus_slice2_qupath_gcs.geojson"
  )
)
#> ℹ 'mg_thymus_slice2_brighter.sirup.rds' is already in '/scratch/f007p0j/RtmpscrZTE/SIRUP_example'.
#> ℹ Downloading 'mg_thymus_slice2_qupath_gcs.geojson'
```

``` r
library(SIRUP)

sirup <- readSIRUP(file.path(extdata, "mg_thymus_slice2_brighter.sirup.rds"))
```

## Draw and export the annotations in QuPath

If you would like to draw the annotations in QuPath yourself, follow
these steps. We do not recommend choosing this route rather than using
`selectSpatialPolygons()` in SIRUP in general, as QuPath does not
natively incorporate gene expression data, and we have found that going
from continuous outlines in QuPath to polygon vertices in SIRUP does not
always work perfectly. Nevertheless, if you have a very large region
that is easy to outline solely with H&E, or if you have a pathologist
who is more comfortable drawing in QuPath, this can be a good option.

1.  Open the full-resolution H&E image in QuPath. It must be the same
    image that the spatial data were registered to. Look for a
    full-resolution TIFF image.
2.  Draw one annotation for each region, and be sure to close every
    outline. Give each annotation a name, such as `GC1`. The name
    becomes the polygon ID in SIRUP. A classification, such as `GC`,
    would also work.

![](figures/qupath-annotations.jpg)

3.  Select the annotations and choose
    `File > Export objects as GeoJSON...`. The menu name can differ a
    little between QuPath versions.

![](figures/qupath-export-menu.jpg)

4.  In the dialog, export the selected objects and keep
    `Export as FeatureCollection` checked. Click `OK` and save the file.

![](figures/qupath-export-dialog.jpg)

QuPath writes the coordinates in pixels of the full-resolution image.
SIRUP will automatically convert them to the coordinates of the object,
which are set as `image_scale` in the object.

## Add the annotations to the object

Use `addQuPathPolygons()` to add the exported annotations to the SIRUP
object, just as you would add polygons drawn using SIRUP with
`addPolygons()`. The function reads the GeoJSON file, converts the
coordinates to the scale of the object, stores the polygons in the SIRUP
object, and adds a `polygon_id` to the `spatial` metadata and
`receptors` table(s).

``` r
geojson <- file.path(extdata, "mg_thymus_slice2_qupath_gcs.geojson")
sirup <- addQuPathPolygons(sirup, geojson)
#> Warning: package 'sf' was built under R version 4.5.3
getPolygons(sirup)
#> # A tibble: 6 × 3
#>   polygon_id vertices           class
#>   <chr>      <list>             <chr>
#> 1 GC1        <tibble [172 × 4]> <NA> 
#> 2 GC2        <tibble [88 × 4]>  <NA> 
#> 3 GC3        <tibble [96 × 4]>  <NA> 
#> 4 GC4        <tibble [182 × 4]> <NA> 
#> 5 GC5        <tibble [235 × 4]> <NA> 
#> 6 GC6        <tibble [282 × 4]> <NA>
table(getSpatial(sirup)$polygon_id)
#> 
#> GC1 GC2 GC3 GC4 GC5 GC6 
#>   7   2   3   6   8  11
```

## Plot the polygons on the tissue

`plotSpatialPolygons()` draws the polygons over the H&E image. It is
worth making this plot every time, because it shows right away if the
annotations and the spots do not line up.

``` r
plotSpatialPolygons(sirup, polygon_alpha = 0.3, label_color = "black")
```

![](qupath-annotations_files/figure-gfm/plot-polygons-1.jpeg)

## Check how the function converts the annotations

`addQuPathPolygons()` has several options and subtleties, which are
worth checking if the polygons you add to the object do not line up
correctly.

- **Scale.** QuPath pixels are full-resolution pixels. The function
  finds the factor that converts them to the coordinates of the object,
  for the `image_scale` of the object. If the object has no
  `image_scale`, it must be given.
- **Buffer.** A spot is a 2D circle, so by default the function expands
  each polygon by the spot radius. A spot whose circle touches the
  outline then counts as inside. Use `buffer = 0` to count only spots
  with center inside the outline (this is not recommended).
- **Names and classes.** The polygon ID is the annotation name. If an
  annotation has no name, the ID is its class and a number, such as
  `GC_01`. Use `class = "GC"` to keep only the GC class.
- **Holes and multipart polygons.** A SIRUP polygon has one ring and
  cannot have holes, so the function drops holes in QuPath polygons and
  gives a warning. A multipart polygon becomes one polygon for each
  part.
- **Existing polygons.** By default, the function adds to the polygons
  that the object already holds. Use `replace = TRUE` to replace them. A
  multi-sample object needs you to pass `sample_id`, and only the
  polygons of that sample change.

To read the annotations without attaching them to an object, use
`readQuPathPolygons()`.

- To build lineage trees and visualize them on the tissue, read
  [Infer clones and lineage trees in situ](clones-and-trees.md).
- To add more sections or bulk AIRR-seq, see
  [Analyze multiple spatial sections and bulk BCR-seq](multisample.md).
- To test spatial patterns, read
  [Choose the right spatial statistic for your question](choose-spatial-statistic.md).

<!-- source: docs/vignettes/regions.md -->

Annotate tissue ROIs and analyze local clonal structure
================

<div markdown="1"
style="background: #F7E5BC; padding: 12px; margin-bottom: 24px; line-height: 24px;">

<p style="margin: -12px -12px 12px; padding: 6px 12px; background: #d6b676; color: #ffffff; font-weight: 700;">

<b>Note</b>
</p>

**Time:** ~15 minutes.<br> **Data:** The example SIRUP object, plus its
polygon file.<br>

</div>

Here, we will select regions of interest (ROIs) on a tissue section,
attach them to a SIRUP object, and examine the BCR repertoire in each
region.

## Load the example object

This code downloads a saved SIRUP object for MG thymus section 2, which
is slightly too big to come directly with the package, and the polygon
file for the section. Change `dest` to a whatever folder you wish to
save the example data in. To see how the object was built, see
[Get started with SIRUP](get-started.md).

``` r
extdata <- SIRUP::downloadSIRUPExample(
  dest = file.path(tempdir(), "SIRUP_example"),
  files = c(
    "mg_thymus_slice2_brighter.sirup.rds",
    "mg_thymus_slice2_gc_polygons.csv"
  )
)
#> ℹ 'mg_thymus_slice2_brighter.sirup.rds' is already in '/scratch/f007p0j/RtmpscrZTE/SIRUP_example'.
#> ℹ 'mg_thymus_slice2_gc_polygons.csv' is already in '/scratch/f007p0j/RtmpscrZTE/SIRUP_example'.
```

``` r
library(SIRUP)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)

sirup <- readSIRUP(file.path(extdata, "mg_thymus_slice2_brighter.sirup.rds"))
sirup
#> <SIRUP object>
#> Spatial data:    Seurat, 3,203 spatial IDs, 449 genes, 1 image
#> Receptor data:   2 slots
#>   BCR: 2,105 receptor sequences x 57 columns; 797/868 receptor IDs in spatial data (91.8%)
#>   TCR: 3,610 receptor sequences x 56 columns; 1,414/1,571 receptor IDs in spatial data (90.0%)
#> Spatial ID field: barcode_10x
#> Clone ID field:  clone_id
#> Analyses:        0
```

## Draw regions

In SIRUP, select ROIs using the `selectSpatialPolygons()` function,
which opens a Shiny app in the web browser. The app shows spots over the
H&E image, colored by a gene or a metadata column in the spatial gex
data. Click to select the vertices of a region, then click **Close
polygon** to join the last vertex to the first. Click **New polygon** to
start the next region. When finished, click **Done**. The app returns a
table of the vertices, and it writes them to the CSV file at
`save_path`.

![](figures/select-spatial-polygons-app.jpg)

The panel on the left sets the assay, layer, and feature (from the
spatial GEX data) that color the spots, the size and opacity of the
points, and whether to show the H&E image and the spots with zero
expression. The screenshot shows one selected polygon.

``` r
gc_vertices <- selectSpatialPolygons(
  sirup,
  feature = "AICDA",
  assay = "alra",
  layer = "data",
  plot_image = TRUE,
  save_path = "mg_thymus_slice2_gc_polygons.csv"
)
```

If you’re working with very large or dense data, like Visium HD these
arguments can help the app respond faster: \* `show_zeros = FALSE` hides
spots with zero expression, which keeps 0 spots from overwhelming the
visualization. \* `downsample_n` draws fewer spots, so the app responds
faster. Each click still snaps to the full set of spots.

<div markdown="1"
style="background: #F7E5BC; padding: 12px; margin-bottom: 24px; line-height: 24px;">

<p style="margin: -12px -12px 12px; padding: 6px 12px; background: #d6b676; color: #ffffff; font-weight: 700;">

<b>Tip</b>
</p>

Give a `save_path`. The CSV file is the record of the annotation, so
other people can repeat the analysis without a second round of drawing.

</div>

### Draw regions on a remote server

If you are running R on a remote server, like an HPC cluster, the app
cannot open a browser on your computer. Instead, start the app on the
server, then connect to it from your computer through an SSH tunnel.

1.  Start R on the server. On a cluster, use an interactive session on a
    compute node (e.g., with `srun --pty`).
2.  Run `selectSpatialPolygons()` with `launch_browser = FALSE` and a
    `port`. Pick a port above 1024 that nobody else on the server uses,
    e.g., 4321.
3.  On your computer, open a second terminal and start the tunnel. The
    tunnel sends your local port to the port of the app. Leave the
    terminal open while you draw.
4.  In the browser on your computer, go to `http://127.0.0.1:4321` (or
    whatever port you chose).

The app runs on the server, but you see it on your computer. When you
finish drawing, click **Done**. The app writes the CSV file on the
server, so provide a `save_path` that is valid there. An example call to
selectSpatialPolygons() is below. The SSH command is also shown. Change
`user` and `server.example.edu` to your username and server.

``` r
# On the server
gc_vertices <- selectSpatialPolygons(
  sirup,
  feature = "AICDA",
  assay = "alra",
  layer = "data",
  plot_image = TRUE,
  save_path = "mg_thymus_slice2_gc_polygons.csv",
  launch_browser = FALSE,
  port = 4321
)
```

``` bash
# On your computer
ssh -L 4321:127.0.0.1:4321 user@server.example.edu
```

If you run R on a compute node behind a login node, the tunnel must
reach the compute node. Add `host = "0.0.0.0"` to
`selectSpatialPolygons()`, so that the login node can connect to the
app, and give the name of the compute node to the tunnel:

``` bash
# On your computer
ssh -L 4321:compute-node-name:4321 user@login.server.example.edu
```

<div markdown="1"
style="background: #F7E5BC; padding: 12px; margin-bottom: 24px; line-height: 24px;">

<p style="margin: -12px -12px 12px; padding: 6px 12px; background: #d6b676; color: #ffffff; font-weight: 700;">

<b>Note</b>
</p>

`host = "0.0.0.0"` lets other computers on the server network reach the
app while it runs. Draw the regions, click **Done**, and let the
function end, so the app does not stay open. Give a `save_path` on the
server, so that the CSV file holds the vertices after the session ends.

</div>

### Read the example polygons

The example data include the polygon file for this section. Read it in
as you would any .csv file.

``` r
vertices <- read.csv(
  file.path(extdata, "mg_thymus_slice2_gc_polygons.csv"),
  colClasses = c(polygon = "character")
)
head(vertices)
#>           spatial_id       x       y polygon         image
#> 1 ATCGACCCAATACAGA-1 300.011 326.595       1 thymus_slice2
#> 2 AGTTCCTATTTATGTT-1 306.874 326.943       1 thymus_slice2
#> 3 CAGTCTGTATACTGGG-1 310.474 320.435       1 thymus_slice2
#> 4 GCGCCGTTCCACGATA-1 306.851 313.941       1 thymus_slice2
#> 5 TTATGAATGAAAGGGA-1 299.989 314.314       1 thymus_slice2
#> 6 ACATCGATCGTTTACC-1 296.388 320.461       1 thymus_slice2
```

Each row is one vertex. `polygon` names the region, `spatial_id` is the
closest spot to where you clicked, and `x` and `y` are its coordinates.

Regions drawn by a pathologist in QuPath (or by you) can be added too,
as shown in [Use QuPath annotations to define ROIs](qupath-annotations.md).

## Attach ROIs to the SIRUP object

Use `addPolygons()` to attach the polygons to the SIRUP object. This
function also automatically annotates the spots and the receptors with
which polygons they live in.

``` r
sirup <- addPolygons(
  sirup,
  polygons_path = file.path(extdata, "mg_thymus_slice2_gc_polygons.csv")
)
sirup
#> <SIRUP object>
#> Spatial data:    Seurat, 3,203 spatial IDs, 449 genes, 1 image
#> Receptor data:   2 slots
#>   BCR: 2,105 receptor sequences x 67 columns; 797/868 receptor IDs in spatial data (91.8%)
#>   TCR: 3,610 receptor sequences x 66 columns; 1,414/1,571 receptor IDs in spatial data (90.0%)
#> Spatial ID field: barcode_10x
#> Clone ID field:  clone_id
#> Analyses:        0
#> Polygons:        9
```

The receptor table and the Seurat metadata now have a `polygon_id`
column. They also have one `TRUE`/`FALSE` column for each polygon, such
as `polygon_5`. This ensures that if you have any overlapping polygons,
you can still identify which polygon each spot or receptor belongs to.

`plotSpatialPolygons()` draws the stored polygons over the tissue.

``` r
plotSpatialPolygons(sirup, polygon_alpha = 0.3)
```

![](regions_files/figure-gfm/plot-polygons-1.jpeg)

Set `zoom = TRUE` to crop the image to the polygons.

``` r
plotSpatialPolygons(sirup, zoom = TRUE)
```

![](regions_files/figure-gfm/plot-polygons-zoom-1.jpeg)

Small polygons can crowd their labels, so set `label_outside = TRUE` to
move the labels outside, each joined to its polygon by a line.

Most SIRUP spatial plots accept `polygons = TRUE`, which draws the
stored polygons on top, as in the next plot of BCR-positive spots.

``` r
plotReceptors(
  sirup,
  slot = "BCR",
  group = "locus",
  colors = "green",
  receptor_size = 1.2,
  receptor_alpha = 0.8,
  polygons = TRUE,
  polygon_alpha = 0.2,
  polygon_color = "white",
  polygon_linewidth = 1,
  zoom = TRUE,
  title = "BCRs and ROI outlines"
)
```

![](regions_files/figure-gfm/receptors-polygons-1.jpeg)

## Overlapping ROIs

ROIs can overlap, e.g., a germinal center can be drawn inside a larger
follicle. To account for this, SIRUP records polygon membership in two
ways

- `polygon_id` holds one region for each spot. If a spot is in more than
  one polygon, it is assigned to the polygon with the smallest area.
- `polygon_<ID>` columns hold the full membership. Each polygon has one
  `TRUE`/`FALSE` column.

SIRUP analyses use `polygon_id` by default for polygon membership. To
use a different rule, build your own column from the `polygon_<ID>`
columns and pass your new column to the analysis functions.

To demonstrate, we will make another polygon around polygon 5.
`expandPolygons()` moves each vertex away from the polygon center by
`delta`, in image pixels.

``` r
expanded_5 <- vertices %>%
  filter(polygon == "5") %>%
  expandPolygons(delta = 12) %>%
  mutate(polygon = "5_expanded")

nested <- addPolygons(sirup, polygons = bind_rows(vertices, expanded_5))

getReceptors(nested, slot = "BCR") %>%
  filter(polygon_5_expanded == TRUE) %>%
  count(polygon_id, polygon_5, polygon_5_expanded)
#> # A tibble: 2 × 4
#>   polygon_id polygon_5 polygon_5_expanded     n
#>   <chr>      <lgl>     <lgl>              <int>
#> 1 5          TRUE      TRUE                  47
#> 2 5_expanded FALSE     TRUE                  65

plotSpatialPolygons(nested, polygon_val = c("5", "5_expanded"), zoom = TRUE, label = FALSE)
```

![](regions_files/figure-gfm/nested-1.jpeg)

The inner polygon is polygon 5 and the outer polygon is the expanded
version. Receptors in polygon 5 keep `polygon_id = "5"`, because polygon
5 is smaller by area. Receptors in the ring around it get
`polygon_id = "5_expanded"`. The `polygon_5_expanded` column is `TRUE`
for both groups.

## Count receptors in each ROI

Use `polygonReceptorSummary()` to count the receptors in each polygon.
It gives one row for each polygon and also stores the table in the
object as an analysis.

``` r
sirup <- polygonReceptorSummary(
  sirup,
  slot = "BCR",
  polygon_id = "polygon_id",
  include_total_spots = TRUE,
  summary_columns = c("c_call", "junction_length"),
  summary_operations = c("cat", "mean")
)

getAnalysis(sirup, "polygon_receptor_summary_BCR")
#>   polygon_id n_receptors n_spatial_ids n_clones top_clone_fraction
#> 1          1          28             6       16          0.1428571
#> 2          2          23             3       16          0.1739130
#> 3          3          14             3        8          0.2857143
#> 4          4           0             0        0                 NA
#> 5          5          47            12       23          0.1276596
#> 6          6           4             4        4          0.2500000
#> 7          7          30             8       12          0.1666667
#> 8          8           6             3        4          0.3333333
#> 9          9           4             3        4          0.2500000
#>                           cat_c_call mean_junction_length n_total_spatial_ids
#> 1        IGHA1,IGHD,IGHG1,IGHG2,IGHM             52.39286                   7
#> 2                   IGHG1,IGHG2,IGHM             54.00000                   3
#> 3            IGHA1,IGHG1,IGHG2,IGHG3             60.64286                   3
#> 4                               <NA>                   NA                   4
#> 5 IGHA1,IGHG1,IGHG2,IGHG3,IGHG4,IGHM             50.29787                  12
#> 6                              IGHG1             62.25000                  11
#> 7                   IGHG1,IGHG2,IGHM             54.90000                   9
#> 8                   IGHA1,IGHG3,IGHM             55.50000                   3
#> 9                         IGHG1,IGHM             52.50000                   3
```

The default output table includes columns that count the receptors, the
spots with receptors, and the clones. The table also gives the fraction
of receptors in the largest clone. `include_total_spots = TRUE` adds the
total number of spots in the polygon.

`summary_columns` and `summary_operations` can add custom summaries.
Pass `summary_columns` a vector of column names in that you want to
summarize from the receptor table, and `summary_operations` a vector of
operations to run on each column. Allowed operations are `count`, `sum`,
`mean`, `median`, `var`, `sd`, `min`, `max`, `any`, `all`, and `cat`. In
the table above, `mean_junction_length` is the mean junction length in
each ROI.

`withPolygons()` runs any function on the receptors of each polygon. It
returns a list with one result for each polygon.

``` r
isotypes <- withPolygons(
  sirup,
  slot = "BCR",
  function(receptors) {
    receptors %>%
      mutate(isotype = substr(c_call, 1, 4)) %>%
      count(isotype)
  }
)
isotypes[["5"]]
#> # A tibble: 3 × 2
#>   isotype     n
#>   <chr>   <int>
#> 1 IGHA       11
#> 2 IGHG       33
#> 3 IGHM        3
```

With `mode = "all_polygons"`, `withPolygons()` runs the function once on
the receptors of all polygons together.

## Determine which clones dominate the ROIs

*Clonal dominance* is the fraction of the receptors in an ROI that
belong to each clone. Use `spatialCloneDominance()` to compute this for
every polygon.

``` r
dominance <- spatialCloneDominance(object = sirup, slot = "BCR", locus_val = "IGH")
names(dominance)
#> [1] "dominance"          "region_spatial_ids" "region_coordinates"
#> [4] "region_receptors"   "polygons"           "metadata"

dominance$dominance %>%
  arrange(polygon, desc(proportion)) %>%
  select(polygon, clone_id, n_receptors, proportion, v_gene_superfamily) %>%
  head(10)
#>    polygon clone_id n_receptors proportion v_gene_superfamily
#> 1        1      928           4 0.14285714              IGHV4
#> 2        1      720           3 0.10714286              IGHV3
#> 3        1      859           3 0.10714286              IGHV4
#> 4        1       17           2 0.07142857              IGHV5
#> 5        1      322           2 0.07142857              IGHV3
#> 6        1      373           2 0.07142857              IGHV3
#> 7        1      519           2 0.07142857              IGHV3
#> 8        1      904           2 0.07142857              IGHV4
#> 9        1        1           1 0.03571429              IGHV5
#> 10       1      128           1 0.03571429              IGHV1
```

The result is a list, and `dominance` is the main table, with one row
for each clone and polygon. The other items hold the spots, coordinates,
receptors, and polygon outlines that the plot functions need. Store the
result in the SIRUP object.

``` r
sirup <- setAnalysis(sirup, "gc_dominance", dominance)
```

By default, each receptor row counts once. Give a numeric column to
`count` to weight the rows, e.g., by `consensus_count`. Set
`exclude_singletons = TRUE` to drop clones with one receptor.

### Plot clonal dominance

`plotSpatialRegionReceptors()` draws the receptors in each polygon,
colored by a column. `top_n` gives a color to each of the most common
values, and the function groups the rest as `Other`.

``` r
plotSpatialRegionReceptors(
  dominance = dominance,
  object = sirup,
  color = "clone_id",
  top_n = 12,
  point_size = 2,
  zoom = TRUE
)
```

![](regions_files/figure-gfm/region-receptors-1.jpeg)

`plotSpatialPolygonPies()` shows each polygon as a pie chart. It has
four modes.

- `"side_by_side"` (default) is a numbered map with the pie charts next
  to it.
- `"spatial_clipped"` fills each pie into its own polygon on the tissue.
  This mode needs the sf package.
- `"dominance_only"` shows the pie charts without a map.
- `"stacked_bar"` shows one stacked bar for each polygon to the right of
  the numbered map.

``` r
pies <- plotSpatialPolygonPies(
  dominance = dominance,
  object = sirup,
  fill = "clone_id",
  top_n = 5,
  label_top_n = 1
)
pies$page_1
#> Warning: Removed 1 row containing missing values or values outside the scale range
#> (`geom_text()`).
```

![](regions_files/figure-gfm/pies-1.jpeg)

The fill column can be any column, not only the clone.
`v_gene_superfamily` shows which IGHV families each region uses. The
`stacked_bar` mode plots a stacked bar chart summarizing the proportions
of each value in each polygon.

``` r
plotSpatialPolygonPies(
  dominance = dominance,
  object = sirup,
  fill = "v_gene_superfamily",
  mode = "stacked_bar",
  top_n = 7
)
```

![](regions_files/figure-gfm/bars-1.jpeg)

The `spatial_clipped` mode draws each pie inside its polygon, which is
not recommended for small polygons as it can be tough to see.

``` r
plotSpatialPolygonPies(
  dominance = dominance,
  object = sirup,
  fill = "clone_id",
  mode = "spatial_clipped",
  top_n = 5,
  zoom = TRUE
)
```

![](regions_files/figure-gfm/clipped-1.jpeg)

## Measure clonal diversity in ROIs

*Clonal diversity* describes the variety and abundance of clones in the
repertoire, see for more details. We are interested in the diversity of
the clones in each ROI.

`polygonDiversity()` calls `alakazam::alphaDiversity()` with polygon as
the grouping variable. `alakazam::alphaDiversity()` resamples every
polygon to the same number of receptors (to ensure comparability, since
diversity is sensitive to sample size), the size of the smallest polygon
that has at least `min_n` receptors, and adds bootstrap confidence
intervals. The function excludes any ROIs with fewer than `min_n`
receptors (default 10). A larger `min_n` gives less noisy estimates but
keeps fewer polygons.

``` r
sirup <- polygonDiversity(sirup, slot = "BCR", polygon_id = "polygon_id", min_n = 10, nboot = 200)
diversity <- getAnalysis(sirup, "polygon_diversity_BCR")
```

The stored analysis is one `alakazam` `DiversityCurve` object, with one
curve for each polygon. Plot it with `alakazam::plotDiversityCurve()`,
which shows the 95% confidence band of each polygon.

``` r
alakazam::plotDiversityCurve(diversity, legend_title = "ROI")
```

![](regions_files/figure-gfm/diversity-plot-1.jpeg)

`summarizePolygonDiversity()` picks one `q` and stores a table with one
row for each polygon. `plotSpatialPolygons()` can then fill each polygon
by a column of any stored analysis.

``` r
sirup <- summarizePolygonDiversity(sirup, slot = "BCR", q = 1, analysis_name = "shannon")

plotSpatialPolygons(
  sirup,
  fill_analysis = "shannon",
  fill_column = "d",
  analysis_fill = c("#08306B", "#FFFF00"),
  polygon_alpha = 1,
  label = FALSE
) +
  labs(fill = "Hill number\n(q = 1)")
```

![](regions_files/figure-gfm/diversity-map-1.jpeg)

`analysis_fill` sets the colors for the lowest and the highest value.
Polygons with too few receptors for the estimate are grey.

`polygonAbundance()` works the same way for clonal rank-abundance
curves. It calls `alakazam::estimateAbundance()` once on all polygons
and stores one `AbundanceCurve`. Plot it with
`alakazam::plotAbundanceCurve()`.

## Extract and compare GEX in ROIs

`seuratSubsetPolygon()` keeps the spots inside polygons and records the
polygon of each spot in the Seurat metadata under the specified column
(e.g., with `metadata = "gc"`). Use it to extract the spots in each
polygon and then make comparisons. Here, we aggregate the expression of
each gene in each polygon to make pseudobulk profiles.

``` r
gc_spots <- seuratSubsetPolygon(sirup, metadata = "gc")
gc_spots
#> An object of class Seurat 
#> 506 features across 55 samples within 2 assays 
#> Active assay: Spatial (449 features, 0 variable features)
#>  2 layers present: counts, data
#>  1 other assay present: alra
#>  1 spatial field of view present: thymus_slice2
table(gc_spots$gc)
#> 
#>  1  2  3  4  5  6  7  8  9 
#>  7  3  3  4 12 11  9  3  3

pseudobulk <- Seurat::AggregateExpression(
  gc_spots,
  assays = "Spatial",
  group.by = "gc"
)$Spatial
pseudobulk[c("AICDA", "MS4A1", "CXCL13", "CD3E"), ]
#> 4 x 9 sparse Matrix of class "dgCMatrix"
#>         g1 g2 g3 g4  g5 g6  g7 g8 g9
#> AICDA    2  .  .  1   4  5   6  .  .
#> MS4A1  107 48 12  6 141 56 258 74 29
#> CXCL13  24 16 14  6  13 12  66 36  7
#> CD3E    11  3  2  2  17 16  12  7  3
```

<div markdown="1"
style="background: #F7E5BC; padding: 12px; margin-bottom: 24px; line-height: 24px;">

<p style="margin: -12px -12px 12px; padding: 6px 12px; background: #d6b676; color: #ffffff; font-weight: 700;">

<b>Note</b>
</p>

Seurat adds a `g` to group names that start with a number. The column
for eGC 1 is `g1`.

</div>

These profiles can be given to a differential expression tool, such as
limma or DESeq2.

## Measure distances between regions

`polygonCentroids()` calculates and returns the centroid of each
polygon. `polygonPairwiseDistance()` returns the distance between every
pair of centroid, in image pixels (`distance`). It also divides each
distance by the diagonal of the section (`normalized_distance`), which
can be used to compare sections of different sizes.

``` r
polygonCentroids(sirup)
#> # A tibble: 9 × 7
#>   sample polygon_id polygon_label     x     y .sirup_y n_vertices
#>   <chr>  <chr>      <chr>         <dbl> <dbl>    <dbl>      <int>
#> 1 <NA>   1          1              303.  320.    -320.          7
#> 2 <NA>   2          2              361.  342.    -342.          4
#> 3 <NA>   3          3              357.  323.    -323.          4
#> 4 <NA>   4          4              429.  369.    -369.          4
#> 5 <NA>   5          5              224.  443.    -443.          6
#> 6 <NA>   6          6              175.  445.    -445.          7
#> 7 <NA>   7          7              173.  391.    -391.          7
#> 8 <NA>   8          8              142.  369.    -369.          4
#> 9 <NA>   9          9              134.  356.    -356.          4
polygonPairwiseDistance(sirup) %>%
  arrange(distance) %>%
  head()
#> # A tibble: 6 × 8
#>   sample  polygon_id_1 polygon_id_2 polygon_label_1 polygon_label_2 distance
#>   <chr>   <chr>        <chr>        <chr>           <chr>              <dbl>
#> 1 spatial 8            9            8               9                   14.5
#> 2 spatial 2            3            2               3                   19.4
#> 3 spatial 7            8            7               8                   38.7
#> 4 spatial 5            6            5               6                   49.5
#> 5 spatial 7            9            7               9                   52.3
#> 6 spatial 1            3            1               3                   53.6
#> # ℹ 2 more variables: normalized_distance <dbl>, section_diagonal <dbl>
```

<!-- source: docs/vignettes/sirup-object.md -->

How the SIRUP object works
================

<div markdown="1"
style="background: #F7E5BC; padding: 12px; margin-bottom: 24px; line-height: 24px;">

<p style="margin: -12px -12px 12px; padding: 6px 12px; background: #d6b676; color: #ffffff; font-weight: 700;">

<b>Note</b>
</p>

**Time:** ~10 minutes.<br> **Data:** A small synthetic SIRUP object
included in the package.

</div>

Here, we will explain the parts of a SIRUP object, the rules that govern
it, and the functions that change the object.

A spatial AIRR-seq (spAIRR) experiment gives us two types of data: gene
expression and adaptive immune receptor sequences measured in spatial
barcodes that map to locations on the tissue. These data need to agree
with each other and be able to interact. The **SIRUP object** keeps the
data in one place and checks these rules.

Because this data is spatially resolved, we are often interested in
studying particular regions of interest (ROIs) on the tissue. The SIRUP
object can also hold such ROIs, which are defined by polygons drawn on
the tissue image.

<div markdown="1"
style="background: #F7E5BC; padding: 12px; margin-bottom: 24px; line-height: 24px;">

<p style="margin: -12px -12px 12px; padding: 6px 12px; background: #d6b676; color: #ffffff; font-weight: 700;">

<b>Note</b>
</p>

This page has very little code. To build an object from real data, see
[Get started with SIRUP](get-started.md) first.

</div>

## Load the example object

The examples use a small synthetic object with 25 spots, 10 genes, 5
clones, and 2 polygons. The spots and gene counts are simulated. The
receptor rows are real BCR sequences from a human thymus section,
assigned to synthetic spots.

``` r
library(SIRUP)

x <- readSIRUP(system.file("extdata", "sirup_synthetic.rds", package = "SIRUP"))
x
#> <SIRUP object>
#> Spatial data:    Seurat, 25 spatial IDs, 10 genes, 0 images
#> Receptor data:   tibble, 36 receptor sequences x 64 columns
#> Spatial overlap: 19/19 receptor IDs in spatial data (100.0%)
#> Spatial ID field: spatial_id
#> Clone ID field:  clone_id
#> Analyses:        0
#> Polygons:        2
```

## Five parts of the SIRUP object

A SIRUP object is an S3 object, and in practice it is a list with five
parts.

| Name | Contents | How to access |
|----|----|----|
| `spatial` | The spatial Seurat object, including gene expression and the H&E image (or named list of spatial Seurat objects) | `getSpatial(x)` |
| `receptors` | The AIRR receptor table, as a tibble (or a named list of tables) | `getReceptors(x)` |
| `metadata` | The important field names (clone_id, sample_id, locus, etc.) and the image settings | `x$metadata` |
| `polygons` | The ROIs that we create, with one row for each polygon | `getPolygons(x)` |
| `analyses` | Analysis results that you want to keep with the object | `getAnalysis(x, name)` |

``` r
getSpatial(x)
#> An object of class Seurat 
#> 10 features across 25 samples within 1 assay 
#> Active assay: Spatial (10 features, 0 variable features)
#>  1 layer present: counts
head(getReceptors(x), 3)
#> # A tibble: 3 × 64
#>   sequence_id spatial_id clone_id locus sequence      rev_comp productive v_call
#>   <chr>       <chr>      <chr>    <chr> <chr>         <lgl>    <lgl>      <chr> 
#> 1 seq01       spot21     1        IGH   CAGGTGCATCTG… FALSE    TRUE       IGHV1…
#> 2 seq02       spot19     1        IGH   CAGGTGCATCTG… FALSE    TRUE       IGHV1…
#> 3 seq03       spot16     1        IGH   CAGGTGCATCTG… FALSE    TRUE       IGHV1…
#> # ℹ 56 more variables: d_call <chr>, j_call <chr>, sequence_alignment <chr>,
#> #   germline_alignment <chr>, junction <chr>, junction_aa <chr>, v_cigar <chr>,
#> #   d_cigar <chr>, j_cigar <chr>, stop_codon <lgl>, vj_in_frame <lgl>,
#> #   c_call <chr>, junction_length <int>, np1_length <int>, np2_length <int>,
#> #   v_sequence_start <int>, v_sequence_end <int>, v_germline_start <int>,
#> #   v_germline_end <int>, d_sequence_start <int>, d_sequence_end <int>,
#> #   d_germline_start <int>, d_germline_end <int>, j_sequence_start <int>, …
getPolygons(x)
#> # A tibble: 2 × 2
#>   polygon_id  vertices        
#>   <chr>       <list>          
#> 1 upper_right <tibble [5 × 2]>
#> 2 lower_left  <tibble [5 × 2]>
```

`summary()` describes each part of the object.

``` r
summary(x)
#> SIRUP summary
#>   Spatial IDs:      25
#>   Receptor records: 36
#>   Receptor IDs:     19
#>   Matched IDs:      19 (100.0%)
#>   Matched records:  36
#>   Image scale:      hires
#>   Swap coords:      FALSE
#>   Stored analyses:  0
#>   Polygons:         2
#> 
#> Per-sample summary
#> # A tibble: 1 × 7
#>   sample  n_spatial_ids n_receptor_records n_receptor_ids n_matched_ids
#>   <chr>           <int>              <int>          <int>         <int>
#> 1 spatial            25                 36             19            19
#> # ℹ 2 more variables: n_matched_records <int>, id_match_rate <dbl>
```

## Set the field names

A receptor table can use any column names, so SIRUP needs to know which
column has what information. It stores this in
`x$metadata$receptor_fields`. There are six key fields:

| Field | Contents |
|----|----|
| `spatial_id` | identifier of the spatial spot that the receptor is in |
| `image` | the name of the Seurat image if the object has multiple images |
| `sample` | the sample name if the object has multiple samples (you would’ve passed a named list to `spatial` during `createSIRUP()`) |
| `clone` | the clone ID |
| `locus` | the receptor locus, such as `IGH` or `TRB` |
| `count` | the number of reads or UMIs supporting the sequence |

``` r
x$metadata$receptor_fields
#> $spatial_id
#> [1] "spatial_id"
#> 
#> $image
#> NULL
#> 
#> $sample
#> NULL
#> 
#> $clone
#> [1] "clone_id"
#> 
#> $locus
#> [1] "locus"
#> 
#> $count
#> NULL
```

The fields are set once, in `createSIRUP()`. After that, SIRUP functions
can find each column without extra arguments. To change a field later,
give a new map to `updateReceptors()` with the `receptor_fields`
argument. A value of `NULL` clears a field.

## Validate the object

`validateSIRUP()` checks that the parts agree. It gives an error if one
of the below rules fails.

1.  The object has class `sirup`.
2.  At least one receptor spatial ID matches a spot name in the Seurat
    object.
3.  Each column that the metadata `receptor_fields` names exists in the
    receptor table. If the object has several receptor tables, the
    spatial ID column must be in every table. Each other named column,
    such as `clone_id`, must be in at least one table.
4.  If the sample field is set, the column exists in every receptor
    table and in the Seurat metadata.

``` r
validateSIRUP(x, verbose = TRUE)
#> <SIRUP object>
#> Spatial data:    Seurat, 25 spatial IDs, 10 genes, 0 images
#> Receptor data:   tibble, 36 receptor sequences x 64 columns
#> Spatial overlap: 19/19 receptor IDs in spatial data (100.0%)
#> Spatial ID field: spatial_id
#> Clone ID field:  clone_id
#> Analyses:        0
#> Polygons:        2
```

`createSIRUP()`, `updateReceptors()`, `updateSpatial()`, and the other
functions that change the object run this check before they return. A
change that breaks a rule fails right away and leaves the original
object as it was.

<div markdown="1"
style="background: #F7E5BC; padding: 12px; margin-bottom: 24px; line-height: 24px;">

<p style="margin: -12px -12px 12px; padding: 6px 12px; background: #d6b676; color: #ffffff; font-weight: 700;">

<b>Note</b>
</p>

SIRUP keeps receptor rows that match no spot, because they could have
come from another experiment. The validation check only requires that at
least one receptor row matches a spot.

</div>

## Set the image settings

Two settings tell SIRUP how to plot spots on the H&E image. Both are
stored in `x$metadata`:

- `image_scale` is the Seurat image scale, `"lowres"` or `"hires"`.
  Choose based on which image you used to build the spatial Seurat
  object when you called `Seurat::Load10X_Spatial()`
- `swap_coords` swaps the x and y coordinates. Some older Seurat objects
  store the coordinates in the opposite order to the image. You can
  check this by grabbing the tissue coordinates with
  `Seurat::GetTissueCoordinates(getSpatial(x))` and comparing them to
  the image (see [Get started with SIRUP](get-started.md) for an
  example). If the tissue is rotated 90 degrees, set
  `swap_coords = TRUE`.

Plotting and spatial statistics functions read these settings when their
own `image_scale` and `swap_coords` arguments are not provided or are
`NULL`, so they only need to be set when you create the SIRUP object.

## Change the data in the object

Because SIRUP cannot possibly wrap every potential tool, it provides a
few functions that let you run other functions on the data inside the
object and update it. These three functions are:

- `updateReceptors(x, fun, ...)` calls `fun(getReceptors(x), ...)` and
  stores the table that `fun` returns.
- `updateSpatial(x, fun, ...)` calls `fun(getSpatial(x), ...)` and
  stores the Seurat object that `fun` returns.
- `updateAnalysis(x, name, fun, ...)` does the same for a stored
  analysis.

Each function validates the object again before it returns. This code
filters out the sequences in clone 3.

``` r
x2 <- updateReceptors(x, dplyr::filter, clone_id != "3")
c(before = nrow(getReceptors(x)), after = nrow(getReceptors(x2)))
#> before  after 
#>     36     29
```

This code adds a column to the Seurat metadata.

``` r
x3 <- updateSpatial(x, function(spatial) {
  spatial$gene_rich <- spatial$nFeature_Spatial >= 8
  spatial
})
table(getSpatial(x3)$gene_rich)
#> 
#> FALSE  TRUE 
#>     2    23
```

Other examples are shown throughout the vignettes. In general, if you
want to update any data in a SIRUP object, you can use one of these
three functions to run your own code on the data and store the result.

## Add regions to the object

See [Annotate tissue ROIs and analyze local clonal structure](regions.md) to learn how to annotate
ROIs and attach them to the SIRUP object.

## Save analyses in the object

`setAnalysis()` stores any R object under a name, e.g., clones, trees,
spatial statistics, and polygon summaries. Stored results then stay with
the SIRUP object for convenience.

``` r
x <- setAnalysis(x, "n_clones", 5)
listAnalyses(x)
#> [1] "n_clones"
getAnalysis(x, "n_clones")
#> [1] 5
x <- removeAnalysis(x, "n_clones")
listAnalyses(x)
#> character(0)
```

## Save and read a SIRUP object

`saveSIRUP()` validates the object and writes it to a .RDS file. The
file also records the version of SIRUP that wrote it. `readSIRUP()`
reads the file and converts an object saved under the old package name
(SIRAP), upgrades an older object to the current layout, warns if the
package versions differ from the file, and validates the object.

``` r
path <- saveSIRUP(x, tempfile(fileext = ".sirup.rds"))
x_again <- readSIRUP(path)
x_again
#> <SIRUP object>
#> Spatial data:    Seurat, 25 spatial IDs, 10 genes, 0 images
#> Receptor data:   tibble, 36 receptor sequences x 64 columns
#> Spatial overlap: 19/19 receptor IDs in spatial data (100.0%)
#> Spatial ID field: spatial_id
#> Clone ID field:  clone_id
#> Analyses:        0
#> Polygons:        2
```

## Storing multiple sets of receptors or spatial data in a SIRUP object

### Multiple receptor tables but one spatial sample

One object can hold more than one receptor table, e.g., one table of
BCRs and one of TCRs. Give `createSIRUP()` a named list of AIRR tables.
Each table is a *slot*. All slots share the spatial data, the polygons,
and the field names. The spatial ID column must be in every table, but a
column such as `clone_id` can be in one table only, e.g., the BCR table.
Clone IDs only need to be unique within one slot. See the example below.

``` r
bcr <- getReceptors(x)
tcr <- bcr[1:8, ]
tcr$locus <- "TRB"

both <- createSIRUP(
  spatial = getSpatial(x),
  receptors = list(bcr = bcr, tcr = tcr),
  spatial_id = "spatial_id",
  clone = "clone_id",
  image_scale = "hires",
  swap_coords = FALSE,
  polygons = getPolygons(x)
)
receptorSlots(both)
#> [1] "bcr" "tcr"
both
#> <SIRUP object>
#> Spatial data:    Seurat, 25 spatial IDs, 10 genes, 0 images
#> Receptor data:   2 slots
#>   bcr: 36 receptor sequences x 64 columns; 19/19 receptor IDs in spatial data (100.0%)
#>   tcr: 8 receptor sequences x 64 columns; 8/8 receptor IDs in spatial data (100.0%)
#> Spatial ID field: spatial_id
#> Clone ID field:  clone_id
#> Analyses:        0
#> Polygons:        2
```

Functions that use receptors work on one slot at a time, chosen with the
`slot` argument. If the object has several slots, `slot` is required. If
the object has only one table, you can leave it out.

``` r
head(getReceptors(both, slot = "tcr"), 3)
#> # A tibble: 3 × 64
#>   sequence_id spatial_id clone_id locus sequence      rev_comp productive v_call
#>   <chr>       <chr>      <chr>    <chr> <chr>         <lgl>    <lgl>      <chr> 
#> 1 seq01       spot21     1        TRB   CAGGTGCATCTG… FALSE    TRUE       IGHV1…
#> 2 seq02       spot19     1        TRB   CAGGTGCATCTG… FALSE    TRUE       IGHV1…
#> 3 seq03       spot16     1        TRB   CAGGTGCATCTG… FALSE    TRUE       IGHV1…
#> # ℹ 56 more variables: d_call <chr>, j_call <chr>, sequence_alignment <chr>,
#> #   germline_alignment <chr>, junction <chr>, junction_aa <chr>, v_cigar <chr>,
#> #   d_cigar <chr>, j_cigar <chr>, stop_codon <lgl>, vj_in_frame <lgl>,
#> #   c_call <chr>, junction_length <int>, np1_length <int>, np2_length <int>,
#> #   v_sequence_start <int>, v_sequence_end <int>, v_germline_start <int>,
#> #   v_germline_end <int>, d_sequence_start <int>, d_sequence_end <int>,
#> #   d_germline_start <int>, d_germline_end <int>, j_sequence_start <int>, …
both <- polygonReceptorSummary(both, slot = "tcr")
listAnalyses(both)
#> [1] "polygon_receptor_summary_tcr"
```

### Multiple spatial samples but one receptor table

`createSIRUP()` accepts one spatial sample (i.e., a spatial Seurat
object) or a named list of spatial Seurat objects, e.g., one for each
tissue section. If you pass a list, the `sample_id` column of the
receptor table matches each receptor row to its corresponding spatial
data, so be sure the names in the list match the values in the receptor
table. Rows with no matching entry stay in the table as non-spatial
records, which is how non-spatial receptors are stored. Spot barcodes
can repeat between sections, so SIRUP matches each receptor to a spot by
the pair of sample and barcode.

``` r
receptors <- dplyr::bind_rows(
  dplyr::mutate(getReceptors(x), sample = "a"),
  dplyr::mutate(getReceptors(x), sample = "b")
)

two_samples <- createSIRUP(
  spatial = list(a = getSpatial(x), b = getSpatial(x)),
  receptors = receptors,
  spatial_id = "spatial_id",
  clone = "clone_id",
  sample_id = "sample",
  image_scale = "hires",
  swap_coords = FALSE
)
two_samples
#> <SIRUP object>
#> Spatial data:    Seurat, 50 spatial IDs, 10 genes, 2 spatial samples, 0 images
#> Receptor data:   tibble, 72 receptor sequences x 65 columns
#> Spatial overlap: 38/38 receptor IDs in spatial data (100.0%)
#> Samples:         2
#> Spatial ID field: spatial_id
#> Sample ID field: sample
#> Clone ID field:  clone_id
#> Analyses:        0
spatialSamples(two_samples)
#> [1] "a" "b"
```

If the sections need different image settings, give named values, e.g.,
`image_scale = c(a = "hires", b = "lowres")`.

### Multiple receptor tables and multiple spatial samples

`createSIRUP()` can accept a named list of receptor tables and a named
list of spatial Seurat objects. Each receptor table just needs a sample
column that matches the names of the spatial Seurat objects. Such
objects follow all of the same rules and conventions as discussed in the
previous sections. Functions that use receptors or spatial data work on
one slot or sample at a time, chosen with the `slot` or `sample`
argument.

### Merging and subsetting SIRUP objects

`mergeSIRUP()` joins several single sample objects into one, with the
sample names that are given.

``` r
merged <- mergeSIRUP(x, x, samples = c("a", "b"), sample_field = "sample")
spatialSamples(merged)
#> [1] "a" "b"
```

`subsetSIRUP()` keeps chosen samples, spots, or receptor rows.

## Next steps

- To build a SIRUP object and run a few simple analyses, see
  [Get started with SIRUP](get-started.md).
- To compare ROIs in the tissue, see
  [Annotate tissue ROIs and analyze local clonal structure](regions.md).
- To add more sections or bulk AIRR-seq, see
  [Analyze multiple spatial sections and bulk BCR-seq](multisample.md).

<!-- source: docs/topics/addQuPathPolygons.md -->

# addQuPathPolygons

## Add QuPath annotations to a SIRUP object as polygons

## Description

`addQuPathPolygons` reads a GeoJSON file that QuPath exported. It converts the annotations to the coordinates of a spatial sample in a SIRUP object. It adds a buffer to each polygon, so that every spot whose circle touches the polygon becomes a member of it. Then it stores the polygons in the object.

## Usage

``` R
addQuPathPolygons(
  x,
  path,
  sample_id = NULL,
  class = NULL,
  keep_unclassified = TRUE,
  image_scale = NULL,
  swap_coords = NULL,
  image = NULL,
  buffer = NULL,
  replace = FALSE,
  include_boundary = TRUE,
  validate = TRUE
)
```

## Arguments

`x`

:   A SIRUP object.

`path`

:   Path to the QuPath GeoJSON file.

`sample_id`

:   Name of the spatial sample that the annotations belong to. A SIRUP object with one spatial sample does not need it. A multi-sample object does.

`class`

:   Class names to keep. If `NULL`, the function keeps all classes.

`keep_unclassified`

:   Keep annotations that have no class (default `TRUE`)? The function ignores this if you set `class`.

`image_scale`

:   Image scale of the polygon coordinates, for example `"hires"`. If `NULL`, the function uses the value stored in `x`. If `x` has no value, you must give one, and the function stores it in `x`. A value that differs from the stored one gives an error.

`swap_coords`

:   Swap the two Seurat coordinate axes? If `NULL`, the function uses the value stored in `x`. The rules are the same as for `image_scale`.

`image`

:   Name of the Seurat image to use. If `NULL`, the function uses the only image of the sample.

`buffer`

:   Distance to grow each polygon, in the coordinates of the object. If `NULL` (default), the function uses the spot radius. Use `0` for no buffer.

`replace`

:   Replace the stored polygons of this sample (default `FALSE`)? If `FALSE`, the function adds the new polygons to the stored ones, and the polygon IDs must not repeat.

`include_boundary`

:   Count spots on a polygon edge as members of the polygon?

`validate`

:   Validate the updated object?

## Details

QuPath writes coordinates in pixels of the full-resolution image. The function finds the factor that converts them to the coordinates of the object. It compares `SeuratObject::GetTissueCoordinates()` at the `image_scale` of the object with the unscaled coordinates. This works for `"hires"` and `"lowres"`. The image that you annotated in QuPath must be the full-resolution image that the spots were registered to.

`image_scale` and `swap_coords` come from the SIRUP object. If the object has no `image_scale`, you must give it. The function swaps the polygon axes in the same way as the spots when `swap_coords` is `TRUE`.

A spot is a circle. By default, the function grows each polygon by the spot radius, which it reads from the scale factors of the Seurat image. If the sample has no Seurat image, the function uses the QuPath coordinates as they are and sets the default buffer to 0. Then [`assignSpatialPolygons()`](assignSpatialPolygons.md) counts a spot as inside when its centre is inside the grown polygon. That is the same as counting every spot whose circle touches the original polygon. Set `buffer = 0` to count only spots with the centre inside the QuPath polygon. For Visium HD, check that the stored spot size suits your bins, or give `buffer`.

A SIRUP polygon cannot have holes. The function drops holes and gives a warning. See [`readQuPathPolygons()`](readQuPathPolygons.md) for the rules about shapes, classes, and IDs.

## Value

The updated SIRUP object. Spatial metadata and receptor records get the new `polygon_id` values.

## See Also

[`readQuPathPolygons()`](readQuPathPolygons.md), [`addPolygons()`](sirup-polygons.md), [`plotSpatialPolygons()`](plotSpatialPolygons.md)

## Examples

``` R
# Write a small GeoJSON file with one annotation. QuPath makes files like it.
geojson <- tempfile(fileext = ".geojson")
writeLines(paste0(
  '{"type":"FeatureCollection","features":[{"type":"Feature",',
  '"geometry":{"type":"Polygon","coordinates":',
  '[[[3.5,0.5],[5.5,0.5],[5.5,2.5],[3.5,2.5],[3.5,0.5]]]},',
  '"properties":{"objectType":"annotation","name":"GC1"}}]}'
), geojson)

x <- readSIRUP(system.file("extdata", "sirup_synthetic.rds", package = "SIRUP"))
x <- addQuPathPolygons(x, geojson, replace = TRUE)
getPolygons(x)
table(getSpatial(x)$polygon_id, useNA = "ifany")
```

<!-- source: docs/topics/addSequenceQualityMetrics.md -->

# addSequenceQualityMetrics

## Add quality measures to an AIRR table

## Description

`addSequenceQualityMetrics` adds columns that can help indicate the quality of each consensus sequence. It keeps all rows.

## Usage

``` R
addSequenceQualityMetrics(
  airr_df,
  sequence = "sequence",
  alignment = "sequence_alignment"
)
```

## Arguments

`airr_df`

:   AIRR-style data frame.

`sequence`

:   Name of the sequence column for the share of called bases (default `"sequence"`).

`alignment`

:   Name of the alignment column for the gap measures (default `"sequence_alignment"`).

## Details

Use this function to look at the distributions of the measures before you choose the thresholds for [`filterAirr()`](filterAirr.md). [`collapseTopConsensusPerSpatialId()`](collapseTopConsensusPerSpatialId.md) also adds these columns, but it removes rows.

The function adds these columns, if the source column exists:

- `non_N_nucleotide_prop`: the share of called bases (`A`, `C`, `G`, `T`) in `sequence`. A low value means an ambiguous consensus. The function takes this value from the ungapped sequence. The alignment would put IMGT gap characters in the denominator.

- `max_gap_length`: the longest run of gap characters in `alignment`.

- `opening_gap_length`: the gap run at the start of `alignment`.

## Value

`airr_df` with the quality columns added.

## See Also

[`filterAirr()`](filterAirr.md), [`collapseTopConsensusPerSpatialId()`](collapseTopConsensusPerSpatialId.md)

## Examples

``` R
x <- readSIRUP(system.file("extdata", "sirup_synthetic.rds", package = "SIRUP"))
metrics <- addSequenceQualityMetrics(getReceptors(x))
head(metrics[, c("non_N_nucleotide_prop", "max_gap_length", "opening_gap_length")])
```

<!-- source: docs/topics/addTissuePositions.md -->

# addTissuePositions

## Add tissue coordinates to an AIRR table

## Description

`addTissuePositions` joins the tissue positions of the spots to an AIRR table. It adds the columns `x` and `y`.

## Usage

``` R
addTissuePositions(
  airr_df,
  positions,
  spatial_id = "spatial_id_8um",
  position_spatial_id = "barcode",
  x = "pxl_col_in_fullres",
  y = "pxl_row_in_fullres",
  keep_position_cols = TRUE
)
```

## Arguments

`airr_df`

:   AIRR-style data frame with a spatial ID column.

`positions`

:   Data frame of tissue positions, or the path of a CSV or parquet file.

`spatial_id`

:   Name of the column in `airr_df` to match (default `"spatial_id_8um"`).

`position_spatial_id`

:   Name of the spatial ID column in `positions` (default `"barcode"`).

`x`

:   Name of the column in `positions` to copy to `x` (default `"pxl_col_in_fullres"`).

`y`

:   Name of the column in `positions` to copy to `y` (default `"pxl_row_in_fullres"`).

`keep_position_cols`

:   Keep all columns of `positions` (default `TRUE`)? If `FALSE`, the result has the columns of `airr_df`, `x`, and `y`.

## Value

A data frame with the columns `x` and `y` added.

## See Also

[`readSpatialIdMapping()`](readSpatialIdMapping.md), [`extractSpatialIds()`](extractSpatialIds.md)

## Examples

``` R
reads <- data.frame(sequence_id = c("a", "b"), spatial_id_8um = c("s1", "s2"))
positions <- data.frame(
  barcode = c("s1", "s2"),
  pxl_col_in_fullres = c(100, 200),
  pxl_row_in_fullres = c(50, 60)
)
addTissuePositions(reads, positions)
```

<!-- source: docs/topics/assignReceptorPolygons.md -->

# assignReceptorPolygons

## Add polygon IDs to a receptor table

## Description

`assignReceptorPolygons` adds polygon columns to a receptor table. It keeps all rows.

## Usage

``` R
assignReceptorPolygons(
  receptors,
  object = NULL,
  polygon = NULL,
  column = "polygon_id",
  spatial_id = NULL,
  images = NULL,
  image_scale = NULL,
  swap_coords = NULL,
  polygon_val = NULL,
  x = "x",
  y = "y",
  receptor_x = "x",
  receptor_y = "y",
  polygon_id = "polygon",
  include_boundary = TRUE,
  slot = NULL
)
```

## Arguments

`receptors`

:   AIRR-style receptor table. You can give a SIRUP object here if you omit `object`.

`object`

:   Seurat object or SIRUP object.

`polygon`

:   Data frame of polygon vertices in order. It needs the columns set by `x` and `y`. If the column set by `polygon_id` exists, the function treats each polygon on its own. If `object` is a SIRUP object and `polygon` is `NULL`, the function uses the stored polygons.

`column`

:   Name of the column to add to the receptor table (default `"polygon_id"`).

`spatial_id`

:   Name of the `receptors` column that holds the spatial IDs. If `NULL`, the function uses the stored field of a SIRUP object, or looks for a standard spatial ID column.

`images`

:   Names of the Seurat images to use.

`image_scale`

:   Image scale for `SeuratObject::GetTissueCoordinates()`. If `NULL`, the function uses the value stored in the SIRUP object.

`swap_coords`

:   Swap the two Seurat coordinate axes? If `NULL`, the function uses the value stored in the SIRUP object. Give a value if `object` is a Seurat object.

`polygon_val`

:   IDs of the polygons to use. If `NULL`, the function uses all polygons.

`x`

:   Name of the x-coordinate column in `polygon` (default `"x"`).

`y`

:   Name of the y-coordinate column in `polygon` (default `"y"`).

`receptor_x`

:   Name of the x-coordinate column in `receptors`, for `object = NULL` (default `"x"`).

`receptor_y`

:   Name of the y-coordinate column in `receptors`, for `object = NULL` (default `"y"`).

`polygon_id`

:   Name of the column in `polygon` that groups the vertices by polygon (default `"polygon"`).

`include_boundary`

:   Count spots on a polygon edge as inside the polygon (default `TRUE`)?

`slot`

:   Name of the receptor slot to use. Leave it `NULL` if the SIRUP object has one receptor table. You must give it if the object has several slots. The function ignores `slot` if you give a plain receptor table.

## Details

If you give `object`, a receptor row gets `NA` if its spatial ID is outside the selected polygons or does not match the spatial object. If `object` is `NULL`, the function finds the polygons from the coordinate columns in `receptors`.

A row in overlapping polygons gets the smallest polygon by area in the primary column. The function also adds one logical column `⁠polygon_<ID>⁠` for each polygon. These columns show membership in every polygon.

If `receptors` is a SIRUP object and you omit `object` and `polygon`, the function uses the stored spatial object and polygons.

## Value

A tibble with the `column` added.

## See Also

[`assignSpatialPolygons()`](assignSpatialPolygons.md), [`withPolygons()`](withPolygons.md)

## Examples

``` R
x <- readSIRUP(system.file("extdata", "sirup_synthetic.rds", package = "SIRUP"))

# Use the spatial object and the polygons stored in the SIRUP object.
receptors <- assignReceptorPolygons(x)
table(receptors$polygon_id, useNA = "ifany")
```

<!-- source: docs/topics/assignSpatialPolygons.md -->

# assignSpatialPolygons

## Add polygon IDs to the spatial metadata

## Description

`assignSpatialPolygons` adds polygon columns to the Seurat metadata. It keeps all spots.

## Usage

``` R
assignSpatialPolygons(
  object,
  polygon = NULL,
  images = NULL,
  image_scale = NULL,
  swap_coords = NULL,
  polygon_val = NULL,
  x = "x",
  y = "y",
  polygon_id = "polygon",
  metadata = "polygon_id",
  include_boundary = TRUE
)
```

## Arguments

`object`

:   Seurat object or SIRUP object.

`polygon`

:   Data frame of polygon vertices in order. It needs the columns set by `x` and `y`. If the column set by `polygon_id` exists, the function treats each polygon on its own. If `object` is a SIRUP object and `polygon` is `NULL`, the function uses the stored polygons.

`images`

:   Names of the Seurat images to use.

`image_scale`

:   Image scale for `SeuratObject::GetTissueCoordinates()`. If `NULL`, the function uses the value stored in the SIRUP object.

`swap_coords`

:   Swap the two Seurat coordinate axes? If `NULL`, the function uses the value stored in the SIRUP object. Give a value if `object` is a Seurat object.

`polygon_val`

:   IDs of the polygons to use. If `NULL`, the function uses all polygons.

`x`

:   Name of the x-coordinate column in `polygon` (default `"x"`).

`y`

:   Name of the y-coordinate column in `polygon` (default `"y"`).

`polygon_id`

:   Name of the column in `polygon` that groups the vertices by polygon (default `"polygon"`).

`metadata`

:   Name of the metadata column that holds the primary polygon of each spot (default `"polygon_id"`).

`include_boundary`

:   Count spots on a polygon edge as inside the polygon (default `TRUE`)?

## Details

A spot outside the selected polygons gets `NA` in the primary column. A spot in overlapping polygons gets the smallest polygon by area. The function also adds one logical column `⁠polygon_<ID>⁠` for each polygon. These columns show membership in every polygon.

## Value

A Seurat object with the `metadata` column added to `⁠@meta.data⁠`.

## See Also

[`seuratSubsetPolygon()`](seuratSubsetPolygon.md), [`assignReceptorPolygons()`](assignReceptorPolygons.md)

## Examples

``` R
x <- readSIRUP(system.file("extdata", "sirup_synthetic.rds", package = "SIRUP"))
flat <- data.frame(
  polygon = "block",
  x = c(3.5, 5.5, 5.5, 3.5),
  y = c(0.5, 0.5, 2.5, 2.5)
)
spatial <- assignSpatialPolygons(
  getSpatial(x),
  polygon = flat,
  image_scale = "hires",
  swap_coords = FALSE
)
table(spatial$polygon_id, useNA = "ifany")
```

<!-- source: docs/topics/assignTipColors.md -->

# assignTipColors

## Assign colors to the tips of clones

## Description

`assignTipColors` gives each tip of each clone a color ID and a color. Tree plots and the matching spatial plots use the same colors.

## Usage

``` R
assignTipColors(
  clones,
  clone_val = NULL,
  clone = "clone_id",
  id = "sequence_id",
  shared_color = NULL,
  palette = NULL
)
```

## Arguments

`clones`

:   Data frame of AIRR data with clone IDs.

`clone_val`

:   Clone IDs to keep before the function assigns the colors. If `NULL`, the function keeps all clones.

`clone`

:   Name of the column that holds the clone IDs (default `"clone_id"`).

`id`

:   Name of the column that holds the sequence or tip IDs (default `"sequence_id"`).

`shared_color`

:   Name of a column. Tips that share a value in this column get the same color within a clone, for example a spatial ID column.

`palette`

:   Vector of colors. If `NULL`, the function uses `pals::glasbey()` if the package is installed. Otherwise, it uses the base R colors from `grDevices::hcl.colors()`.

## Details

The function numbers the tips of each clone in the order of `id`. If you give `shared_color`, tips with the same value of that column get the same number within a clone. For example, tips in the same spot get the same color.

## Value

A data frame with the columns `tip_color_id` and `tip_color` added.

## See Also

[`plotSpatialCloneTreePairs()`](plotSpatialCloneTreePairs.md)

## Examples

``` R
x <- readSIRUP(system.file("extdata", "sirup_synthetic.rds", package = "SIRUP"))
colors <- assignTipColors(getReceptors(x), shared_color = "spatial_id")
head(colors[, c("clone_id", "spatial_id", "tip_color_id", "tip_color")])
```
